9a97847a97d012ebc2aea8f9.title_original: Rethinking "RL Generalizes, SFT Memorizes": The Role of SFT Data
9a97847a97d012ebc2aea8f9.excerpt: arXiv:2611.14912v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Large language models trained with Reinforcement Learning (RL) with verifiable rewards exhibit strong reasoning ability and broad generalization, whereas models trained with Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) are often viewed as more prone to memorization and limited transfer. This paper rethinks this distinction through the lens of SFT training data on widely used Qwen2.5 and Qwen3 series models. First, we study the role of data source and show that it is critical: a carefully mixed SFT dataset substantially outperforms data generated solely by a larger model. Second, we study the role of data scale and show that matching the number of correct rollouts between SFT and RL greatly improves SFT generalization, while matching the total rollout budget enables SFT to generalize as well as RL. Combining these two factors further enables SFT to generalize even better than RL. Third, by using LLM annotations to characterize the solution methods in training rollouts, we show that larger datasets cover more tail methods and that these tail methods provide generalizable reasoning signals. Finally, we support these empirical findings theoretically by analyzing the training dynamics of shallow transformers under both RL and SFT.

189eb90f2e9023c58470510e.title_original: ReShap: Interpretable Reinforcement Learning for High-Dimensional Multi-Action Settings
189eb90f2e9023c58470510e.excerpt: arXiv:2611.15507v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Deep Reinforcement Learning (RL) plays a crucial role in tackling complex tasks, yet its reliance on deep neural networks makes the learned policies opaque. To enhance the trustworthiness of RL policies, existing work (e.g., the SILVER framework [Li et al., 2025]) has focused on Shapley-based interpretability, but is typically restricted to low-dimensional state spaces, binary-action settings, and a single class of linear surrogate. We propose ReShap, a policy-distillation framework that extends Shapley-based interpretability to high-dimensional, multi-action environments. ReShap extracts compact feature representations from raw image observations, performs SHAP-based feature attribution to characterize how each feature contributes to the policy's decisions, and distills the deep RL policy into an interpretable surrogate trained on the full set of (state, policy-action) pairs along the policy's visited distribution. We instantiate the surrogate with three interpretable model families (decision trees, linear regression, and logistic regression) and compare their fidelity and task return. We evaluate ReShap on Atari and Box2D environments using three deep RL algorithms and conduct a human-subject study to assess the clarity and trustworthiness of the resulting policies. Results show that ReShap preserves competitive task performance, that decision trees generally outperform linear and logistic regression, and that linear

e61e078d8268121795153042.title_original: Spec-Driven PBT: Deriving Semantic Invariants from Code Specifications for Agentic Property-based Testing
e61e078d8268121795153042.excerpt: arXiv:2611.15920v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Software is increasingly written by AI agents that produce an implementation from a natural language specification, a practice known as agentic coding. Code is now produced faster than it can be reviewed, and has been shown to exhibit its own characteristic failure patterns. Property-based testing (PBT), a long-standing technique in which invariant properties of a program are checked against many generated inputs, has recently been revisited with LLM agents authoring the properties, thereby removing the high-effort derivation of invariants that has long hindered its adoption. Existing methods, however, derive these properties from the implementation alone (Code-driven PBT). At the same time, a thorough specification such as a product requirements document has become routine within agentic coding, yet its role in testing the resulting code remains underexplored. We study the value of the specification as a source of properties for testing agent-written code. Our key insight is that the specification, unlike the implementation, records what the code was meant to do, and invariants derived from it are not biased by particular implementation choices. We propose Spec-Driven PBT, an agent that first expresses invariants in natural language from the specification and only then inspects the implementation to translate them into concrete tests. Across 25 applications from ViBench, Spec-Driven PBT finds a novel set of bugs that

8dc0463306a6887c20fb17cc.title_original: EgoX: Egocentric Cross-Embodiment Manipulation with Embodiment Dreaming
8dc0463306a6887c20fb17cc.excerpt: arXiv:2611.16728v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Generalist manipulation policies can benefit from the complementary experience of humans, real robots, and simulated agents. However, differences in morphology, sensing, and control interfaces make it difficult to learn effectively from their combined demonstrations. We introduce EgoX, an egocentric cross-embodiment learning framework that shares manipulation structure through fine-grained, semantically corresponding observation and action modalities while keeping sensing and control interfaces embodiment-specific. EgoX pretrains a Modular Embodiment Dreamer (MED) on this mixture and fine-tunes it on target-embodiment demonstrations. Within each embodiment, MED assigns a dedicated tokenizer to each observation modality and a dedicated expert to each action modality, with a Transformer trunk shared across embodiments. A training-only embodiment-dreaming objective predicts latent representations of future visual and proprioceptive states, encouraging the shared trunk to model each embodiment's dynamics. Across 13 task-embodiment pairs spanning five tasks and six robot embodiments, including five physical robots and one simulated humanoid, cross-embodiment pretraining raises MED's average normalized task progress from 0.63 to 0.80 over training from scratch. The gains are particularly pronounced under out-of-distribution conditions, where average task progress increases from 0.53 to 0.77. Ablations demonstrate the benefit

248fb3e6aa83cc8553bd8d61.title_original: A Critical Appraisal and Motivated Intruder Test of A Search Dataset Anonymised for the Purposes of the EU Digital Markets Act
248fb3e6aa83cc8553bd8d61.excerpt: arXiv:2611.21689v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This study evaluated the European Commission's anonymisation measures for Alphabet's search-data sharing under Article 6(11) of the Digital Markets Act against European Data Protection Board guidance and contemporary practice, and assessed re-identification through motivated intruder testing. The measures focus on search end-users, leaving other individuals mentioned in queries insufficiently protected, and do not explicitly address inference. The accompanying controls and safeguards reflect good practice for managing residual risk. Motivated intruder testing targeted 98,501 individuals across six countries using publicly available profiles. Google-verified matches yielded a re-identification rate of 0.094%, below the study's 0.47% per-team threshold. Each verified match required about three hours (Euro 105), excluding Google verification and Gemini costs, suggesting limited cost deterrence. All country-level rates were below the threshold, but one region exceeded it. The threshold drew on conservative precedents, adjusted for data quality, verification, controls and safeguards, assuming five independent attack teams. Some sensitivity scenarios exceeded the threshold, but relied on strong assumptions, such as treating all uncertain matches as correct. Results may not generalise beyond the targeted population, and ethics requirements constrained the attacks. Personal data detection recall was assumed rather than tested: the minim

a5946ac087f71129743cde0b.title_original: Threat Landscape of Vibe Coding and the Road to Secure Autonomy
a5946ac087f71129743cde0b.excerpt: arXiv:2611.21822v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Vibe coding is reshaping software development, enabling faster implementation and allowing individuals with limited programming experience to describe requirements in natural language while AI agents write, test, and deploy the code. As these agents evolve into autonomous systems that execute commands, manage dependencies, access cloud resources, and interact with other agents, their security risks extend beyond incorrect code to actions with direct consequences for software systems. Although research on these risks is expanding, it remains fragmented across areas including prompt injection, insecure code generation, supply-chain attacks, and human factors, with limited consensus on terminology, threat assumptions, and evaluation. This paper consolidates emerging research through the lens of the vibe coding workflow. We establish a reference architecture, characterise six levels of agent autonomy, and develop a threat model centred on five trust boundaries spanning developers, AI models, tools, cloud infrastructure, and the wider software ecosystem. Building on this foundation, we propose a taxonomy of twenty-one threats across nine classes. For each threat, we review the available evidence, assess proposed defences, and identify limitations. Our analysis highlights that risks increase with agents' operational authority, while most defences rely on model judgement and address isolated threats. Finally, we identify eleven researc

f78b09a513b7d62d2b659c09.excerpt: arXiv:2611.21883v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Much of the web is funded by advertising, a model that erodes as humans delegate browsing to AI agents acting on their behalf. A natural replacement is for agents to pay for what they consume, often a fraction of a cent per request. At the scale of web traffic, this could mean tens or even hundreds of millions of payments per second. We present Bajillion, a clearing protocol for scalable micropayments. A sender signs a payment request, and an untrusted operator answers with a preconfirmation, which promises the receiver that it will be paid. Periodically, the operator closes an epoch by posting only the net effect of its payments on chain. Bajillion guarantees that a malicious operator can only omit payments -- it can never debit a sender beyond what it signed, nor misdirect a transfer. Posted balances are therefore finalized immediately and can be withdrawn. By design, senders never have to raise disputes, making it suitable for ephemeral AI agents. A receiver that is shortchanged can prove that a close omitted a preconfirmed payment, which halts the protocol and lets every user exit with its finalized balance. Requests from different senders can be processed independently, allowing the operator to parallelize up to the number of senders. We capture these guarantees in an ideal functionality for accountable clearing and prove that Bajillion realizes it.

e9ec692233e818851d230ae0.title_original: A Forensic Analysis of Metadata and Information Leakage in Swedish Public Documents
e9ec692233e818851d230ae0.excerpt: arXiv:2611.21922v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This study investigates metadata and structural content leakage in publicly available PDF documents from 30 Swedish public-sector authorities. Using an automated collection pipeline and ExifTool-based extraction, 2,876 documents were analyzed and classified using an R0-R3 risk taxonomy. Results reveal that 48.4% of documents exhibit significant metadata exposure (R2 or R3), with significant variation across institutional tiers (p < 0.001). Longitudinal analysis across three legislative periods reveals a statistically significant reduction in metadata exposure between the baseline and post-enactment periods, yet 44.9% of documents published after the enactment of the Swedish Cybers\"akerhetslagen continue to leak sensitive metadata. Furthermore, 41.6% of documents contain incremental update layers; forensic analysis recovered verifiable text alterations, including deleted personal data and internal identifiers, from 228 of these cases. These findings highlight persistent regulatory lag and a systemic reliance on default, unsanitized document publication workflows within the Swedish public sector.

6803bb6a1cca90f892a76194.title_original: CNN Architecture Comparison for Malware Classification with Limited Training Data
6803bb6a1cca90f892a76194.excerpt: arXiv:2611.21936v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Traditional malware classification methods struggle to keep pace with rapidly evolving threats. Image-based malware classification offers a promising alternative by converting malware binaries into grayscale images for analysis with deep learning. While effective, organizations often face practical constraints in acquiring sufficient training data, especially for newer threats. This thesis investigates dual-path CNN architectures with intermediate feature fusion as a potential enhancement for malware classification, with particular focus on how varying training data size affects their comparative performance against traditional single-path approaches. This research implements and compares two models: a baseline single-path using the pre-trained VGG16 architecture and a dual-path model that combines VGG16 with a custom CNN through intermediate feature fusion. Both architectures are evaluated on a binary classification task distinguishing between two malware families (C2Lop.P trojan and Dialplatform.B worm) from the Malimg dataset. Each model is trained across four different training data proportions (20%, 40%, 60%, and 80%), with three training runs per size to ensure statistical robustness, while being evaluated on complementary test sets of varying sizes. 778175b1f6a4224d4b9cd6b6.title_original: PersonaHate: A Scalable Persona-Based Data Synthesis Pipeline for Hate Speech Analysis
778175b1f6a4224d4b9cd6b6.excerpt: arXiv:2611.21951v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Hate speech remains a persistent and evolving threat on online platforms. The widespread use of large language models (LLMs) further intensifies this problem by making hateful content easier and cheaper to generate at scale. Although stronger hate speech detectors continue to be proposed, their performance remains uneven across target identity groups and different forms of hateful expression, partly because existing training data provides only limited coverage of these cases. Thus, we introduce PersonaHate, a scalable persona-driven data synthesis pipeline for constructing diverse hate speech datasets. PersonaHate begins with a large persona pool of 457K personas drawn from two real-world sources. Conditioned on selected personas from this pool, it prompts eight LLMs to generate hate speech across 34 identity groups and performs multi-judge annotation to obtain reliable labels. The resulting corpus contains 791K samples, from which we curate a 67K group-balanced training set. Our modular design also supports extension to new identity groups, generators, and emerging hate targets. Built upon this dataset, we evaluate two detector training strategies: training from scratch and further fine-tuning. Results show that all trained models achieve competitive performance across four widely used external benchmarks. Notably, a 184M-parameter DeBERTa-v3 model trained on PersonaHate reaches 77.5% average F1 and 79.4% average accuracy, outp

b17aa53e3fc8ba6a44e53b55.title_original: Hierarchical Personalized Federated Learning for Fine-Grained Intrusion Detection: A Multi-Class Analysis in Heterogeneous Attack Environments
b17aa53e3fc8ba6a44e53b55.excerpt: arXiv:2611.21970v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Intrusion Detection Systems (IDS) play a vital role in protecting modern network infrastructures. Although Federated Learning (FL) enables collaborative training without sharing raw network traffic, global models struggle with non-IID attack distributions. Moreover, practical security operations require fine-grained attack classification for targeted threat responses. To address these challenges, this paper investigates the convergence dynamics and performance of Hierarchical Personalized Federated Learning (HPFL), which combines multi-tier aggregation with client-level personalization, for 8-class, 6-class, and 4-class intrusion detection using Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) models implemented in NVIDIA FLARE on the CICIDS2017 dataset. Experimental results show that personalized HPFL models achieve micro F1-scores up to 0.9911 in the 6-class task, while the overall local accuracy reaches 0.9975 in the 8-class task. On 8-class local test sets, HPFL achieves a micro F1-score of 0.9901 and a macro F1-score of 0.8324, outperforming FedAvg (0.7176) and FedProx (0.5624) in macro F1. Cross-client evaluations demonstrate out-of-distribution generalization, with HPFL achieving a 4-class micro F1-score of 0.9294 compared with 0.9140 for standalone local models. Furthermore, distance-weighted network analysis estimates a 48.9% reduction in transmission overhead compared with conventional FL (194.4 MB vs. 380.3 MB for the 8-class task). Thes

4ed16e6e5f55983a53d8f66b.title_original: Is 4-Bit Quantization More Than Noise to a Chat Model's Safety Behaviour? Attributing Behavioural Shifts with Matched Perturbations
4ed16e6e5f55983a53d8f66b.excerpt: arXiv:2611.22186v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Chat models on phones and laptops are usually 4-bit copies of the model that was evaluated, and audits of such copies disagree about what quantization does to refusal. A 4-bit build is one of many weight perturbations of the same size, so a change in its behaviour could come from its specific rounding error or from any perturbation that large. In a pre-registered study of three 3-4B chat models, with paired tests, blind human labels and an 8-bit null, we find two 4-bit shifts of opposite sign: with a compliant reply prefilled, Qwen2.5-3B continues into harmful content more often, and on held-out jailbreaks Llama-3.2-3B complies 10.3 points less often. Matched perturbations separate the two. Shuffled and Gaussian versions of the error average close to zero, while scaling the real error, from its mirror image to twice its size, changes behaviour near-linearly. At half the real error, Llama's likelihood is almost unchanged, yet it already complies 5.8 points less often, and llama.cpp's Q4_K_M, at the same bits per weight, moves neither model. Refusal under 4-bit quantization depends on the specific rounding error, not on bits per weight or likelihood, so each build has to be compared with its original.

3117cd97a937f750bda47e02.title_original: GapLeak: When Privacy-Preserving LLM-based Web Agents Become a Privacy Risk
3117cd97a937f750bda47e02.excerpt: arXiv:2611.22223v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large Language Model (LLM)-based web agents rely on data minimization and least privilege to protect user privacy. We show that these principles are necessary but insufficient: they constrain authorized sources, but not higher-sensitivity sources that remain reachable. A website can request a field unavailable from authorized sources, creating an information gap. To complete the task, a goal-driven agent may escalate to reachable but unauthorized sources and disclose accumulated sensitive information. We formalize this vulnerability as GapLeak, where an adversary exploits a legitimate web form without prompt injection or other malicious instructions. We evaluate GapLeak on three web-agent frameworks and six LLMs from Anthropic, Google, and OpenAI across recruitment, e-commerce, travel, and healthcare. GapLeak induces an average unauthorized disclosure of approximately 37%. The information gap is the primary driver: eliminating it reduces disclosure by more than 50%. Existing instruction-level defenses based on least privilege partially mitigate the vulnerability but often reduce task success. We propose submission-time verification, which filters unauthorized content before form submission, eliminating over 96% of unauthorized disclosures while preserving task success.

4ff80c01477e2ea63231e3a6.title_original: From Token Changes to Task Failures: Bit Flips in a Shared KV-Cache Block
4ff80c01477e2ea63231e3a6.excerpt: arXiv:2611.22243v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In LLM serving systems with prefix caching, each KV block of a shared system prompt is held in GPU memory as a single physical copy, which every request with that prompt reads. Our earlier work measured change and showed that one bit flip in such a block changes many later responses without making them visibly degenerate. This paper extends that work by measuring how often the changed responses are wrong. Using software fault injection into vLLM serving Qwen3-8B, we flip the most significant mantissa bit or the sign bit of a value in such a block. We score responses on four tasks: code generation, short-answer questions, multiple-choice reasoning, and refusal under a policy. The fraction of changes that turned a correct response wrong depended strongly on the task: 0.023 on MBPP+ and 0.59 on held-out TriviaQA at the mantissa bit, and 0.019 and 0.60 at the sign bit. Harm fell on requests whose sampled answers are sometimes wrong, so the damage of a flip depends on how common such requests are. Harmed responses looked like ordinary errors, so a flip should be detected by checking cached blocks rather than by monitoring outputs.

3959a3f7ed3b5a63e0da414b.title_original: Dressed in Authority: Practical Black-Box Jailbreaking of MLLMs via Visual Trust Bias
3959a3f7ed3b5a63e0da414b.excerpt: arXiv:2611.22292v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) are rapidly advancing, yet their safety remains a critical concern, especially under jailbreak attempts. Existing MLLM jailbreaks either inject fragile adversarial perturbations into irrelevant images or synthesize toxic visual cues to achieve text-driven attack intents. In contrast, a more practical MLLM jailbreak emphasizes enhancing attack efficacy directly on naturally occurring harmful image-text pairs. We address this problem by proposing Visual Trust Bias Attack (VTBA), a new jailbreak framework that exploits a previously overlooked attack surface: MLLMs exhibit an intrinsic trust bias toward authoritative visual features, which enables transferable and stealthy jailbreaks. VTBA constructs a bank of authoritative templates, matches each input pair to the most relevant one, and integrates the harmful intent into the selected layout, thereby leveraging credible visual cues to override safety refusals while preserving naturalness. We further construct a dataset of 2,500 naturally occurring image-text pairs to evaluate jailbreaks in this practical multimodal setting. Extensive experiments show that our method consistently achieves high attack success rates across strong MLLMs, revealing a severe and previously underexplored weakness in current multimodal safety alignment. Warning: This paper may contain sensitive content.

ddb8df822a5c7df25825a457.title_original: TetherMark: Instance-Level Watermark Authentication Against Cross-Instance Transplantation
ddb8df822a5c7df25825a457.excerpt: arXiv:2611.22345v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Robust watermarking is commonly verified by asking whether a hidden payload remains decodable after compression, geometric distortion, or generative editing. Localized and semantic extensions may additionally check whether an expected region or category is still present. These tests establish evidence validity or content consistency, but not whether the evidence still belongs to the particular visual instance registered by its owner. We expose cross-instance transplantation: an attacker extracts or estimates valid watermark evidence from one registered image and transfers it to a different image of the same category. The message can still decode, the expected content can remain present, and the result can look natural, even though the evidence has been reassigned to the wrong instance. To enable instance-level watermark authentication, we introduce TetherMark, a post-hoc watermark that combines two complementary checks. The message check verifies an edit-robust payload, while the relation check uses secret patch-pair selection, a registered response, natural correspondence transport, and enrollment normalization to test consistency with the registered instance. The verifier accepts only when both checks pass. Across 240 test subjects, TetherMark attains 92.08% legitimate true acceptance with 9.17% and 16.25% attack success under WmForger and WMCopier, respectively, yielding the highest instance-binding balanced accuracy under bo

32725a3ae67a8048c698c304.title_original: From Attack Tree to Model Checker: Binding CAPEC Patterns to Verify Robotic System Security
32725a3ae67a8048c698c304.excerpt: arXiv:2611.22408v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Security-minded verification of autonomous and robotic systems presupposes an attacker, yet the path from a threat catalogue to a checkable attacker model is still traversed by hand. This research preview presents the theory and construction of a pipeline that mechanises it. Each leaf of an attack tree is mapped to a CAPEC attack pattern and written in first-order logic as a rule: the attacker's prerequisites imply the attack's effect. Casting the pattern as such a rule is what makes it operational - its variables can be bound to a specific system's parts, and its prerequisites can then be tested against that system under a chosen configuration of security controls. Binding is our means of verifying whether a system is vulnerable to a given attack: from a bound pattern we derive an attacker model, turn its effect into a temporal-logic property, and check that property against the system with and without a countermeasure, reporting the control that defeats the attack. We describe the signature, schemas, profiles for approach, and explore how CAPEC can support reasoning about robotics security.

de9461d3e3b5cf1e52eafb77.title_original: Exploited Before It Was Fixed? Vulnerability Timelines from Open, Machine-Readable Evidence
de9461d3e3b5cf1e52eafb77.excerpt: arXiv:2611.22479v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: -05-X-03), Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalogs, and exploitation sightings. We introduce an evidence model implemented in Vulnerability-Lookup that selects the earliest evidence for each lifecycle event, distinguishes vulnerability-specific records, preserves date precision, and ensures traceability to original sources. Among 3,758 vulnerability identifiers with exploitation evidence, 98% have disclosure dates, while only 15.7% have patch evidence. Vendor-side dates required by VTEM are entirely absent. Most exploitation dates originate from catalog listings, including 1,041 entries associated with bulk catalog imports. After excluding these entries and ambiguous same-day observations, 59 vulnerabilities exhibit patch evidence following exploitation evidence, with a median interval of 7.6 days, predominantly between catalog listings and distributor fixes. Evidence traceability also exposes systematic measurement errors: one collector incorrectly classified exploit publications as active exploitation, accounting for 40% of initial exploitation dates, while another catalog assigned vulnerability publication timestamps to 11% of its listings. Our findings demonstrate that exploitation-to-patch intervals are computationally measurable, but their reliability depends on the availability, precision, and provenance of published evidence. ecb1aa84cd4c4f5857c8aae1.title_original: How Well Is My Artwork Protected? Predicting and Tailoring Protection against Style Mimicry by Personalization
ecb1aa84cd4c4f5857c8aae1.excerpt: arXiv:2611.22486v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Protection tools add an imperceptible perturbation to each artwork so that a model personalized on it fails to imitate its style, and they apply one recipe, a protection method at a fixed strength, to every artwork. We find that the same recipe protects artworks very differently, well beyond the noise of personalization seeds, and that cheap signals predict this protection before any personalization. Because protection rises and falls together across recipes, our method, Patina, predicts the protection of every recipe from one short trial protection and gives each artwork the weakest recipe whose predicted protection reaches a chosen level. At the same level of visibility, Patina lets more artworks pass the protection threshold than any single recipe and warns the artist about artworks for which no recipe is predicted to pass it.

9093103f84e1155e99a05cb4.title_original: Flexibility Has a Price: Quantifying Modality Policies in Maliciously Secure Multi-Biometric Authentication
9093103f84e1155e99a05cb4.excerpt: arXiv:2611.22714v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Multi-biometric authentication improves robustness and accessibility by combining information from multiple biometric modalities. Existing research has primarily focused on secure multimodal authentication, feature fusion, and recognition performance, while paying comparatively little attention to the security implications of modality-flexible authentication policies. At the same time, most systems provide limited cryptographic protection for biometric data during authentication. This paper addresses both challenges. We first study modality flexibility as a security decision rather than merely a usability feature. Each accepted modality subset creates an authentication entry point, and the resulting risk depends on the joint behavior of all accepted subsets and the attempt budget. We introduce a framework for quantifying this security cost and develop a policy-selection procedure that identifies policies satisfying a target risk level while supporting users who can present only a subset of modalities. We then present SUPERMBA, a two-server privacy-preserving authentication system that enforces the selected policy without revealing biometric templates or the modality subset used in an authentication attempt. The protocol provides verifiable policy enforcement even when one server is malicious and executes the same computation irrespective of the chosen policy or modality subset. Experiments on the three-modality MULB+ dataset sho

f41a831739a77ddeded5e835.title_original: Provable Mixing Properties of Parallel Mixnets Revisited
f41a831739a77ddeded5e835.excerpt: arXiv:2611.22732v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A mix-network (mixnet) is a routing network that breaks source-to-destination message trackability by indistinguishably mixing the routes of concurrently transmitted messages, thus providing anonymity to senders, receivers and sender-receiver pairs. Given their potential use in high-stakes scenarios like protecting whistleblowers, one would like to prove formally that sender anonymity holds in a mixnet, even against strong adversaries that can compromise subsets of mixnet servers. However, existing work on anonymity in mixnets is either limited to linear mixnets (which do not scale horizontally), relies on special provisions such as additional noise or chaff messages, or is empirical -- typically based on entropy, which does not provide strong guarantees if the adversary has auxiliary information. In this paper, we present a new analysis of parallel mixnets which scale horizontally, showing that these networks can provide strong indistinguishability for messages even without additional noise messages. Our analysis works by bounding the statistical variance of the adversary's posterior likelihood of where a message of interest is at a given point in time. Using concentration bounds on this distribution, we show that parallel mixnets satisfy $(\varepsilon, \delta)$-differential indistinguishability for messages routed through the mixnet (similar to $(\varepsilon, \delta)$-differential privacy) with very small failure probabilities

2f5bc5db71bd36b1b5bf2081.title_original: Guarded Swarms in the Loop: A ROS 2/PX4 Digital Twin for Hybrid Digital-Analog Coordination of UAV/UGV Swarms
2f5bc5db71bd36b1b5bf2081.excerpt: arXiv:2611.22773v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Swarms of unmanned aerial and ground vehicles (UAV/UGV) operating in contested environments cannot rely on software alone for physical safety, since the software stack and its networks are part of the attack surface. The Guarded Swarms architecture addresses this by pairing a digital coordination layer, built on Topic-Based Communication Space Petri Nets (TB-CSPN), with an independent analog safety layer that can veto unsafe actuation commands. So far, the architecture has been specified and argued for, but not executed. We present the first executable instantiation of Guarded Swarms as a digital twin built on ROS 2, the PX4 autopilot in software-in-the-loop mode, and Gazebo, with two UAVs and one UGV in a coastal counter-UAS scenario. The TB-CSPN transition chain, from multi-modal sensing through human authorization to vehicle tasking, is mapped one-to-one onto ROS 2 nodes, and the analog layer is modeled as a per-vehicle Virtual Safety Board that gates every command. Eight groups of experiments show that the three negative guarantees of the architecture (no mission from conflicting, temporally incoherent, or unauthorized evidence) hold at three distinct stages of the chain in all 60 counterfactual runs; that threat confirmation is bounded by the narrowest sensing modality; that the safety layer exercises its full modeled envelope independently of the coordination layer; and, under fault injection, that it prevents every collis

92810be3a3dbb1d8fab943d4.title_original: CaFe: Causally Faithful Conditional Traffic Scenario Generation
92810be3a3dbb1d8fab943d4.excerpt: arXiv:2611.22855v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Language-conditioned traffic simulation enables scalable test scenarios steered by natural language. The goal is to control selected agents while surrounding traffic reacts to their observed behaviour. For example, a vehicle instructed to cut in late should cause the following vehicle to brake only when the manoeuvre becomes observable. Yet simulators can leak private instructions across agents, causing surrounding vehicles to react before the instructed behaviour becomes observable. Such premature reactions defuse desired events and alter the ensuing closed-loop scenario. Existing benchmarks measure what agents do, not what they could have known, leaving this failure unmeasured. We formalise it as intent leakage and address it through evaluation, data and modelling. Our paired intervention test holds an instructed agent's executed trajectory fixed while varying its private instruction, isolating leakage-induced changes in surrounding agents. We also construct WOMD-PACT, an automatically generated, verifiable dataset of 531,099 WOMD scenes with timed behaviour tags with reaction episodes identified through a counterfactual ghost test and grounded private instructions. Finally, we introduce CaFe, a dual-stream diffusion-forcing simulator fine-tuned in closed loop that restricts inter-agent interactions to public beliefs, preserving legitimate anticipation without leaking private intent. Our evaluation reveals that existing condit

957b6f3d25686b91b914cd19.title_original: Can Verifiable PIR Match the Online Efficiency of SimplePIR?
957b6f3d25686b91b914cd19.excerpt: arXiv:2611.22911v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Verifiable Private Information Retrieval (vPIR) ensures that a malicious server cannot return tampered database records, but it traditionally incurs significant overhead compared to classical PIR.Recent advancements, notably VeriSimplePIR, approach the online efficiency of SimplePIR by introducing a proof preprocessing phase and requiring only lightweight client-side online verification. However, this scheme relies on an additional Short Integer Solution (SIS) assumption and SIS-based commitments, which only support relaxed range proofs. Consequently, these schemes are forced to adopt significantly weaker parameter choices, resulting in additional online overhead. In this paper, we propose a novel vPIR protocol that employs a newly designed error-correcting code-based commitment scheme as the database digest. This approach (i)supports efficient proofs of linear relations, (ii) achieves precise range proofs and (iii) eliminates the reliance on the SIS assumption. Thus, our scheme successfully adopts parameter choices identical to those of SimplePIR. As a result, our vPIR protocol is the first to achieve exactly the same online communication and server computation costs as SimplePIR, while keeping online client computation nearly identical. Additionally, compared to VeriSimplePIR,our protocol reduces online communication and client-side computation by approximately 20%, and decreases online server-side computation by over 35%.

d52494b4fdf879209a826a3d.title_original: On Improving the Adoption, Usability, and Retention of Static Application Security Testing (SAST) Tools
d52494b4fdf879209a826a3d.excerpt: arXiv:2611.21621v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: As the Internet connects more of the world, software vulnerabilities create growing security risks. Because software developers are responsible for building and maintaining secure applications, they rely on tools and techniques that help identify vulnerabilities early in development. Static Application Security Testing (SAST) tools analyze source code to identify potential security weaknesses before software is deployed. Although SAST can help developers address vulnerabilities proactively, these tools also present usability and adoption challenges. This thesis examines those challenges and explores ways to improve the adoption, usability, and continued use of SAST. First, a literature review of 89 research works related to SAST implementation and continued usage identifies recurring developer concerns, including false positives and other usability barriers that can reduce trust in SAST results. Second, the thesis presents a process for automating the execution of SAST tools and formatting their output so that findings are more meaningful and actionable to developers. A real-world use case evaluates an implementation of this process and gathers developer feedback. Participants reported satisfaction with several aspects of the process and indicated that it increased their willingness to use the SAST tool.

4a3295d3d71e9aea125ae862.title_original: Wrong Input, Wrong Threshold: Re-evaluating Adversarial Facial Privacy
4a3295d3d71e9aea125ae862.excerpt: arXiv:2611.21923v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Published face-privacy methods report protection above 90% against black-box recognition models. That number comes from an evaluation protocol with two independent defects, reported in a measure that cannot size either one. The input is wrong: methods published since 2022 feed the network the whole photograph, or a detector's box, where deployed systems detect, align to a landmark template and crop. Re-scoring the same files through a realistic front end costs a standard transfer attack 56% of its dodging protection and a budget-allocating attack 7%, with no image regenerated. The measure is wrong: that loss is a difference of success rates, so it saturates, moving by 8.2x over a budget sweep while the effect beneath it moves by 1.34x. We therefore report the paired cosine shift, in which both thresholds cancel algebraically, so the input defect holds without committing to a calibration. Measured that way it is 2.2x and 10.7x larger on three unseen recognizers, and at matched budget it reverses the L-infinity transfer ranking: the one surveyed method that aligns at evaluation gains 0.18 where MI-FGSM loses 0.05. The cause is a resampling mismatch, not perturbation lost outside the crop; optimising through a differentiable alignment operator largely removes it, adding +24 to +58 points on unseen recognizers and a commercial system, with a residual on one of them. The thresholds are wrong: the four constants inherited since 2021

df088a1de53476fc0fa0575a.title_original: GuardAgent: A Memory-Augmented Agentic Framework for Adaptive Detection of Adversarial Promotions in LLM-Based Recommendation
df088a1de53476fc0fa0575a.excerpt: arXiv:2611.22274v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: In traditional recommender systems (RSs), textual information typically serves as auxiliary signals for representation learning. In contrast, in LLM-based RSs, textual information becomes the primary medium for recommendation generation through semantic understanding and reasoning. This shift fundamentally changes the attack surface, making promotion-driven manipulations more feasible, effective, and harder to detect. However, effectively detecting such attacks remains largely unexplored. To fill this gap, we present the first systematic study on detecting promotion-driven attacks against LLM-based RSs, aiming to safeguard next-generation recommendation platforms. Specifically, we propose GuardAgent, a novel LLM-powered agentic detection framework that operates through a loop of Perception, Action, Reflection and Memory. In contrast to conventional LLM-based detectors that function in a static, one-off, and opaque fashion, GuardAgent continually learns and self-evolves to adapt to unseen threat patterns while generating explainable reasoning traces and outcomes. Extensive experiments on real-world datasets demonstrate that GuardAgent achieves state-of-the-art generalization performance, laying the foundation for robust and trustworthy recommendation in practical settings.

9af096bcacb162d8936d1712.title_original: A Little Advice Suffices: Diffie-Hellman Is as Hard as Discrete Logarithm
9af096bcacb162d8936d1712.excerpt: arXiv:2611.22290v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Is computing a Diffie-Hellman key as hard as computing a discrete logarithm? Maurer showed that it is, given a few bits of advice, provided that short intervals contain enough integers with only small prime factors; that proviso has stood for thirty years. We remove it. For every prime $p$ there is an advice string of $O(\log p)$ bits, depending only on $p$, with which discrete logarithms in every group of order $p$ are computed in polynomial time from a Diffie-Hellman oracle. The reduction is the classical one; what was missing was a proof that short intervals contain polylogarithmically smooth integers. We show that a zero-free half-plane for the Riemann zeta function, which is now known, gives the expected number of $(\log x)^K$-smooth integers in every interval $[x,x+x^\theta]$ with $\theta>17/30$. With smoothness this small the saddle point of the counting integral lies just to the left of the line $\mathrm{Re}\,s=1$, and a zero-free strip of any fixed width absorbs the shift once $K$ is large. Genus-2 Jacobians, whose orders fill such intervals, then turn one of these integers into the order of an auxiliary group. The same input removes the smoothness assumption from Maurer and Raub's impossibility of field-homomorphic one-way permutations and from the yes/no-query reduction of Koblitz, Menezes and Shparlinski. It also makes Wolf's characterisation unconditional: discrete logarithm and Diffie-Hellman are generically equi

ed7d35e36bba6df9b129ce93.title_original: Fast and Strong Image Protection against Diffusion Personalization
ed7d35e36bba6df9b129ce93.excerpt: arXiv:2611.22494v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Personalized text-to-image diffusion models can reproduce a person from a handful of photographs. Image protection perturbs each image before publication so that fine-tuning on it fails, but it optimizes every perturbation from scratch, so its cost grows with the number of images. We present the protective diffusion model (PDM), which is trained once and samples the perturbation of a new image over many denoising steps. PDM distills an iterative teacher and is then post-trained with the target residual projection (TRP) loss as a reward, a stronger objective than existing ones. PDM outperforms nine baselines on faces and artworks and nearly matches its teacher at a tenth of the cost.

950ba0d8bf614a5f1148fb94.title_original: Missing Security-Fix Backporting for GitHub Actions Workflows
950ba0d8bf614a5f1148fb94.excerpt: arXiv:2611.22519v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: GitHub natively supports workflow automation through GitHub Actions, now the dominant CI/CD tool on the platform. Yet keeping these workflows secure remains an ongoing burden: maintainers often patch a vulnerability on the default branch but leave the same flaw on the release and maintenance branches that downstream consumers continue to build from. Carrying a known fix onto these divergent branches, called backporting, is rarely done, and this paper presents the first large-scale empirical study quantifying the resulting gap. From a public corpus of GitHub Actions workflow histories, we mine 1,903,191 workflow-modifying commits, scan each before and after with the static scanner zizmor to identify 69,865 security fixes across 24,238 projects, and audit every release branch to check whether each fix was carried over. The gap is pervasive: 224,392 of 474,490 audited release branches remain vulnerable, and deliberate backporting is rare and slow, with only 19,476 of 78,907 already-fixed branches confirmed as plausible backports at a median lag of 243 days. We thus design WorkflowBP, the first technique for automated security-fix backporting of GitHub Actions workflows. WorkflowBP takes a neuro-symbolic approach: it compiles a default-branch fix into a domain-specific representation called the Workflow Semantic Patch (WSP) and applies it to each divergent branch by matching jobs and steps based on their content rather than their

ffa48ba2eda9d315fef36e5b.title_original: Propose with the Gradient, Accept with the Loss: One Hedged Attack for Pixel-Sparse Robustness
ffa48ba2eda9d315fef36e5b.excerpt: arXiv:2611.22596v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: A pixel-sparse adversary may change a few pixels of an image to any value. Robustness to such attacks is currently measured with an ensemble, sparse-AutoAttack (sAA), because its members fail in different places: sparse projected gradient descent (sPGD) trusts a first-order model that a full pixel change breaks, and sparse random search (Sparse-RS) ignores the gradient even where it is informative. We show that both attacks are local searches, each a proposal distribution plus an acceptance rule, and ask what such a search can learn from the gradient. A Taylor bound says what to measure, and measurements at the states the search visits give five rules. The sign of the gradient is its most reliable use at a single pixel and sets a new pixel's value. Its ranking of candidate pixels should be followed loosely, and its ranking of the pixels to remove, which is often more reliable, can be followed more closely. A pixel should not be proposed twice before a move is accepted, and acceptance should be decided by the loss alone. These rules define Gradient-guided Random Search (GRS), which runs once and costs one forward and one backward pass per step. On 13 CIFAR-10 configurations and 5 ImageNet models, GRS matches or beats the best single member of sAA and is within one point of sAA itself or stronger on 17 of 18 settings, and it is significantly stronger than sAA on 8. It uses 3 instead of up to 7 forward-pass units, and on CIFAR-10

a1bc8d1ad8135e1c7e13e9d8.title_original: Who Pays for Byzantine Robustness? Validity, Data-Share Dictatorships, and Fairness When Only a Few Hospitals Collaborate
a1bc8d1ad8135e1c7e13e9d8.excerpt: arXiv:2611.22904v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Clinical federated learning (FL) collaborations typically connect only three to six hospitals, yet Byzantine-robust aggregation rules are designed and benchmarked on synthetic partitions across dozens of equal-sized clients. We conduct an empirical audit of eight standard aggregation rules: FedAvg, coordinate-wise median, trimmed mean, Krum, Multi-Krum, Bulyan, geometric median (GeoMed), and Centered Clipping (CC). We evaluate both unweighted and sample-size-weighted variants across three cross-silo medical datasets from the FLamby benchmark: Fed-Heart-Disease ($n = 4$ hospitals), Fed-TCGA-BRCA ($n = 6$ regions), and Fed-ISIC2019 ($n = 6$ centres). We execute 54,214 training runs across enumerated attacker coalitions ($f \in \{1, 2\}$) paired with exact-twin leave-out controls that decompose performance drops into honest data loss versus adversarial attack damage. We report three findings. First, client-count validity checks fail to capture breakdown in skewed medical consortia: while $n = 6, f = 1$ satisfies every count condition except Bulyan's, assigning sample-size weights turns median and GeoMed into a clean-model dictatorship whenever a single hospital holds more than half the training data, and causes weighted median, GeoMed, and CC to collapse when that dominant centre attacks. 22a1b0ea104cabc549569431.title_original: Dissecting the GPU Load/Store Unit and Exposing Its Security Risks
22a1b0ea104cabc549569431.excerpt: arXiv:2611.23022v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: GPUs are the main platform for large-scale machine learning and power the largest supercomputers. Their load/store units (LSUs) often determine kernel performance and have been exploited in prior attacks. Yet what is known about the LSU is only a few isolated mechanisms and parameters, and even a single one has been enough for an attack. In particular, it is still unknown what a load costs, where loads contend, and even whether a warp can starve due to contention. Until each is measured, neither its security risk nor a defense is known. We reverse-engineer how the LSU serves load instructions on recent NVIDIA GPUs with microbenchmarks and analyze the security implications. We give a cycle-accurate latency formula for a global L1 hit or shared memory access from the addresses it touches, whose address-dependent terms are bank conflicts and the L1 tag lookup; we show that loads contend at both, and that when the LSU pipeline is full a warp can starve a warp of a later-launched block. We then show that the LSU's attack surface is far broader than prior attacks revealed: through channels never exploited before, it can leak information, communicate covertly, and degrade colocated workloads. Through either global bank conflicts or tag lookups alone, we recover a full AES-128 key under the threat model of prior GPU AES timing attacks. 79cce814d2426bea4dc52ae7.title_original: Distortion-Free Semantic Watermarks for Black-Box Generative Models
79cce814d2426bea4dc52ae7.excerpt: arXiv:2611.23208v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We present a provably distortion-free semantic watermarking algorithm that requires only black-box sampling access to a generative model and black-box access to a semantic embedding. Conventional such watermarks are often brittle to transformations. This is especially problematic for images, where benign operations such as compression, cropping, or resizing change the entire pixel representation. Semantic watermarks therefore require detection to be robust to content-preserving transformations. Previous methods combining these properties rely heavily on specific white-box properties of the underlying model: either to autoregressive text generation or to diffusion-specific access, such as control of the initial noise or diffusion inversion. In contrast, our construction is fully generic: It only interacts with the generative model and the semantic embedding, a function that determines the notion of "preserving content" under which detection should be robust, via sample and query access. We then instantiate this framework for image generation. 544c3fad2ed8892113f301ec.title_original: HE-LRM: Encrypted Deep Learning Recommendation Models using Fully Homomorphic Encryption
544c3fad2ed8892113f301ec.excerpt: arXiv:2506.18150v5 Announce Type: replace Abstract: FHE inference systems primarily target models with dense inputs, while Deep Learning Recommendation Models (DLRMs) contain sparse categorical features that require lookups into embedding tables. Encrypted lookups are challenging because indexing is not natively supported and must be expressed using SIMD arithmetic. A direct one-hot formulation does not scale. Prior work addresses parts of this problem through embedding compression or compact encrypted queries. However, it does not address complete DLRM inference, leaving open how private lookup interacts with downstream computation and memory constraints. We present HE-LRM, the first end-to-end FHE system for private DLRM inference. We use deterministic compositional embedding compression with client-side digit decomposition, avoiding expensive homomorphic selector construction while consuming only one multiplicative level. We further develop a block-diagonal packing strategy that performs lookups across multiple embedding tables using optimized BSGS linear transformations and produces encrypted embeddings directly compatible with downstream inference. We extend Orion with a high-performance GPU backend and achieve 9 ms for single-inference embedding lookup. We also show that GPU memory capacity limits batching and therefore the latency-bound throughput in such systems. 4aa15cfb72fec11288778a4d.title_original: PSM: Prompt Sensitivity Minimization via LLM-Guided Black-Box Optimization
4aa15cfb72fec11288778a4d.excerpt: arXiv:2511.16209v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: System prompts are critical for guiding the behavior of Large Language Models (LLMs), yet they often contain proprietary logic or sensitive information, making them a prime target for extraction attacks. Existing defense mechanisms frequently rely on heuristics, incur substantial computational overhead, or are inapplicable to models accessed via black-box APIs. This paper introduces a novel framework for hardening system prompts through shield appending, a lightweight approach that adds a protective textual layer to the original prompt. Our core contribution is the formalization of prompt hardening as a utility-constrained optimization problem. We leverage an LLM-as-optimizer to search the space of possible SHIELDs, seeking to minimize a leakage metric derived from a suite of adversarial attacks, while simultaneously preserving task utility above a specified threshold, measured by semantic fidelity to baseline outputs. This black-box, optimization-driven methodology is lightweight and practical, requiring only API access to the target and optimizer LLMs. We demonstrate empirically that our optimized SHIELDs significantly reduce prompt leakage against a comprehensive set of extraction attacks, outperforming established baseline defenses without compromising the model's intended functionality. 00977a48d8bade8862b6f93e.title_original: IH-Benchmark: A Conflict-Centered Benchmark for Instruction-Hierarchy Robustness in Large Language Models
00977a48d8bade8862b6f93e.excerpt: arXiv:2607.25987v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: When a language model receives conflicting instructions from different priority levels, which one does it actually follow? This question lies at the heart of reliable LLM deployment. We present IH-Benchmark, a conflict-centered benchmark for instruction-hierarchy robustness across direct System $\succ$ User (S $\succ$ U) conflicts and tool-mediated User $\succ$ Tool (U $\succ$ T) conflicts. We organize tests into seven constraint categories according to the higher-priority requirements under evaluation. Each test is evaluated with a uniform binary pass/fail protocol combining a predicate domain-specific language (DSL) with rubric-based LLM judges. We report category-balanced compliance rates and evaluate non-conflict controls separately. Our evaluation of 32 model configurations over five runs each reveals substantial variation in overall compliance, with scores ranging from 32.9% to 97.8%. Models achieve higher compliance on S $\succ$ U than on U $\succ$ T on average, at 84.6% and 69.6%, respectively. Strong performance on the former track does not guarantee comparable robustness on the latter. 88f382e61f19204f1ee57d31.title_original: A Deployment-Oriented and Resource-Efficient Neuro-Symbolic Framework for Explainable DDoS Detection in Operational Technology Networks
88f382e61f19204f1ee57d31.excerpt: arXiv:2608.16769v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: This paper presents a hybrid neural-symbolic detector of distributed denial-of-service (DDoS) attacks on the availability of operational technology (OT) networks, designed for their resource-constrained gateways, and an evaluation matched to deployment. The evaluation on CIC-DDoS2019, Edge-IIoTset and CICIoT23 uses contiguous or capture-held-out partitions, dependence-aware intervals, and precision and alert load at operational prevalence. Over ten seeds at a 1% budget, the hybrid's false-negative rate on CIC-DDoS2019 is 0.08%, against 0.26% for the GRU and 0.17% for the tree. With a day of mostly unseen attack families held out, the tree alone carries the decision. Audits bound these claims: Edge-IIoTset is saturated by duplicates, no benchmark as used provides interleaved traffic in capture order, and an unconstrained tree is more accurate on two of them, so the case for the hybrid rests on short, stable rules and a measured footprint. 49e5b9b811e4fbed9938b650.title_original: IoMT-SecAlarmBench: A Semi-Synthetic Counterfactual Benchmark for Integrity Attacks in IoMT
49e5b9b811e4fbed9938b650.excerpt: arXiv:2608.26416v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The Internet of Medical Things (IoMT) combines clinical physiological data with cyber-system information, creating challenges in determining whether an abnormal reading reflects a genuine physiological event, a device fault, or a cyber-attack within the expected physiological range. Answering this requires counterfactual ground truth, which no existing dataset provides. We present IoMT-SecAlarmBench, a semi-synthetic benchmark that injects controlled integrity attacks into genuine coupled ECG+PPG recordings using a structured experimental design combining four attack morphologies, four severity levels, two physiological plausibility conditions, and replay attacks. Each injected window retains its cause, attack subtype, and the clean signal that would have been observed without the attack. We evaluate six detectors from five method families using threshold-independent measures and a matched false-alarm budget. Results show no method consistently detects the most difficult cases: replay attacks and low-amplitude transient spikes remain close to chance-level performance across detectors. Results also reveal a trade-off between detecting attacks and distinguishing them from sensor faults: the best-performing detector on hard cases flags fault/artifact windows at 5.3 times its false-alarm rate on normal data. 2982b0a7bca20a81d48339e6.title_original: rApp/xApp Attestation: A New Security Use Case for O-RAN
2982b0a7bca20a81d48339e6.excerpt: arXiv:2609.24296v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The disaggregation and softwarization introduced by the Open Radio Access Network (O-RAN) architecture enable multi-vendor innovation but also expose the RAN Intelligent Controller (RIC) ecosystem to new runtime security risks. Existing O-RAN specifications define strong safeguards for onboarding, authentication, identity management, and secure communication; however, they do not provide a concrete mechanism for verifying whether deployed rApps and xApps remain in their intended, untampered state during operation. This paper introduces rApp/xApp attestation as a RIC-native O-RAN security use case for runtime integrity verification. Rather than proposing a new cryptographic protocol, the work defines how existing integrity verification techniques can be integrated into O-RAN through attestation modules, attestation agents, RIC application interfaces, and SMO-driven policy coordination. We map the use case to relevant O-RAN Alliance working groups, identify required standardization extensions, and demonstrate feasibility through a lightweight hash-based prototype implemented on the Near-RT RIC platform. 50d192290cf241bcf1a17748.excerpt: arXiv:2611.15019v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Encrypted tunnels are widely used to circumvent censorship, which has drawn censors' efforts to detect and block them. As the circumvention tunnels in widest use have largely converged on TLS, detection has shifted from the content of their traffic to its shape, where recent research and real-world blocking events have revealed exploitable fingerprints of tunneling. Existing traffic-shaping obfuscators such as obfs4, however, are fundamentally limited in hiding these fingerprints, as their application-driven design can only add to the shape that the application creates. A schedule-driven obfuscator, which decides when and how much to send independently of the application, can give tunnels any shape but raises new challenges, first and foremost what a good shape is. This paper presents obfsgen, a schedule-driven obfuscator for tunneling traffic. obfsgen samples its schedule from a generative sequence model of normal traffic, which predicts the future shape of a flow from its whole history, to capture the long-range dependencies that make a flow's shape normal. Built around this model, obfsgen addresses system problems that such an obfuscator faces in practice, such as synchronization across a noisy network. We evaluate the (in)distinguishability that obfsgen offers, the performance overhead that it adds and the computational resources that it requires. We see the schedule-driven architecture as the next generation of tunnel o

8759240898661ce9da415901.title_original: CoordX Types: A Trustless, Swappable Type System for Shared Records
8759240898661ce9da415901.excerpt: arXiv:2611.16128v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The CoordX Protocol carries signed and encrypted entries between parties. It proves who wrote each entry and who had permission to write it. It does not say what an entry means. That task belongs above the protocol layer. This paper describes the CoordX type system, the layer that gives entries a meaning. A type is a short document that says how to read one part of a shared record: which entries count, what each position means, what a party may do there, and what a party must do next. The type system has two key properties. It is trustless: a type is an ordinary signed object fixed by its digest, and every party evaluates it for itself over entries that the CoordX Protocol has already verified. No party has to trust a server, a registry or another party's software. It is swappable: a type names the interpreter it is written for, so many interpreters, of different capabilities and designs, can be used side by side in one record. We describe how to write type schemas, and we define the expressive power of the schema language. Payloads form a regular language. Entry structure forms a regular tree language. Every rule and every computed value is a total function in the primitive recursive class, so evaluation always halts. We compare this with KQML, FIPA-ACL and CBCL, and we relate it to language-theoretic security.

8135a3149820ce7612fbeb8b.title_original: RustMC: Automated Verification of Real-World Concurrent Rust
8135a3149820ce7612fbeb8b.excerpt: arXiv:2502.06293v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: RustMC is a stateless model checker that targets push-button verification of unmodified concurrent Rust programs. As both Rust and C/C++ compile to LLVM IR, RustMC builds on GenMC which provides a verification framework for LLVM IR. This allows verification of Rust code and any foreign function dependencies. In this tool paper we present key implementation challenges, use-cases, and an empirical evaluation of RustMC. The challenges include intercepting threading operations, promoting memory intrinsics, and handling uninitialised accesses, all stemming from Rust's unique compilation strategy. Case studies adapted from real-world programs show RustMC finds concurrency bugs in unsafe Rust code, FFI calls to C/C++, and atomic operations. We evaluate our tool's functionality on the Loom model checker test suite and a set of production-level Rust concurrent data structures.

However, the security vulnerabilities exhibited by the visual modality pose significant challenges to deploying such models in open-world environments. Recent studies have successfully induced harmful responses from target MLLMs by encoding harmful textual semantics directly into visual inputs. However, in these approaches, the visual modality primarily serves as a trigger for unsafe behavior, often exhibiting semantic ambiguity and lacking grounding in realistic scenarios. In this work, we define a novel setting: vision-centric jailbreak, where visual information serves as a necessary component in constructing a complete and realistic jailbreak context. Building on this setting, we propose the VisCo (Visual Contextual) Attack. VisCo fabricates contextual dialogue using four distinct vision-focused strategies, dynamically generating auxiliary images when necessary to construct a vision-centric jailbreak scenario. To maximize attack effectiveness, it incorporates automatic toxicity obfuscation and semantic refinement to produce a final attack prompt that reliably triggers harmful responses from the target black-box MLLMs. Specifically, VisCo achieves a toxicity score of 4.78 and an Attack Success Rate (ASR) of 85% on MM-SafetyBench against GPT-4o, signifi

ebe56384c5905a7e9d0e2eb7.title_original: Angelfish: Leader, DAG, or Anywhere in Between
ebe56384c5905a7e9d0e2eb7.excerpt: arXiv:2509.15847v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: To maximize performance, many modern blockchain systems rely on eventually synchronous, Byzantine fault-tolerant (BFT) consensus protocols. Two protocol designs have emerged in this space: protocols that minimize latency using a leader that drives both data dissemination and consensus, and protocols that maximize throughput using a separate, asynchronous data dissemination layer. Recent protocols such as Partially Synchronous Bullshark and Sailfish combine elements of both approaches by using a DAG to enable parallel data dissemination and a leader that paces DAG formation. This improves latency while achieving state-of-the-art throughput. Yet leader-based protocols still achieve better latency under moderate loads, which are common in practice. We present Angelfish, a hybrid protocol that adapts smoothly across this design space, from leader-based to Sailfish-like DAG-based consensus. Angelfish lets a dynamically adjusted subset of parties use best-effort broadcast to issue lightweight votes instead of reliably broadcasting costlier DAG vertices. This reduces communication, helps lagging nodes catch up, and lowers latency in practice compared to prior DAG-based protocols. Our empirical evaluation shows that Angelfish attains state-of-the-art peak throughput while significantly lowering latency under moderate load, delivering the best of both worlds.

758b93f101267b78c0cd8b9b.title_original: Concave is the New Linear: Sybil Attacks Collapse Anti-Plutocratic DAO Voting
758b93f101267b78c0cd8b9b.excerpt: arXiv:2605.18990v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Decentralized Autonomous Organizations (DAOs) run protocol governance by letting token holders vote on proposals. For concave rules actually proposed to dampen governance power -- those that are positive, increasing, and finite -- we show that the optimal strategy yields power that is asymptotically linear in token holdings, regardless of the cost scheme. 2a4120b2a677cee3639a4548.title_original: Tight Lower Bounds for Differentially Private Continual Counting
2a4120b2a677cee3639a4548.excerpt: arXiv:2609.17650v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: The Binary Tree Mechanism is a standard algorithm for differentially private continual counting, but its complete asymptotic optimality under differential privacy has remained unresolved since its introduction. We resolve this question. For $0 \leq \varepsilon \leq 1$, we prove asymptotically tight lower bounds for $\ell_\infty$, mean squared, and maximum per-coordinate expected squared error simultaneously under all regimes of $0 \leq \delta \leq 1/4$. These bounds hold for arbitrary mechanisms, even when the entire stream is available in advance. Our lower bounds match the (blocked) Binary Tree Mechanism instantiated with the best of Laplace or Gaussian noise, establishing its asymptotic optimality. Our proof uses a single hard distribution where elements are ``tagged'' as potentially being the target flipped element via a score evaluated down a tree. A simple modification of the score allows the same framework to establish tight lower bounds for all three error measures.

669aaae20844c209ea4cbdac.title_original: Optimal Additive Integer Masks for One-Guess Vulnerability under an Absolute-Moment Budget
669aaae20844c209ea4cbdac.excerpt: arXiv:2611.16066v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We study the average one-guess success probability of an adversary who observes the ordinary integer sum of a finite-support secret and an independent integer-valued mask, subject to an absolute-moment budget on the mask. For a uniform secret on an interval the exact optimum and an explicit optimiser are obtained. For a biased bit the masks that achieve no increase over the prior baseline are characterised, and the entire cost--vulnerability frontier is determined. It is the piecewise-linear interpolation of an explicit sequence of points generated by cost-optimally shifted truncated geometric masks. It has infinitely many affine pieces, which accumulate at the critical cost, where the frontier meets the prior baseline with zero slope. The proof rests on a layer-cake decomposition of an arbitrary mask into truncated geometrics, along which both the vulnerability and the cost are exactly additive. The results give exact design guidance for additive integer noise under the average one-guess metric.

ed695ca7f6e34bc7113bc07d.title_original: The challenge of defending against bulletproof dead drops on public blockchains
ed695ca7f6e34bc7113bc07d.excerpt: The evolution of malware command-and-control (C2) infrastructure has shifted away from fragile, centralized servers and hardcoded domains toward resilient, decentralized blockchain networks that eliminate single points of failure. Threat actors are leveraging immutable public ledgers such as Bitcoin transactions, EVM smart contracts via techniques like EtherHiding, TRON wallets, and Solana memo programs to store, mask, and persistently update their operational endpoints. By executing read-only remote procedure call (RPC) queries to retrieve encrypted C2 configurations directly into compromised endpoint memory, adversaries can continuously bypass traditional perimeter defenses and domain seizures. Modern cybersecurity requires a fundamental shift away from static domain blocklists toward monitoring anomalous outbound JSON-RPC traffic, analyzing endpoint memory, and treating blockchain infrastructure as an active threat communication channel. The command-and-control (C2) channel is the operational backbone of any persistent malware campaign. It is also the most fragile component. The moment an actor's C2 infrastructure is identified and reported to the hosting provider, the domain registrar, or law enforcement, the campaign's operational capability collapses. 7bfd7a1d711f081c03eca426.title_original: Goodhart in the Planner: Sampling-Based Control Exploits Rewards Learned from Human Preferences
7bfd7a1d711f081c03eca426.excerpt: arXiv:2611.09670v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Robots increasingly plan by searching against a reward model learned from human preferences. We measure what this search does to the true objective. On HalfCheetah and Hopper with crowd-sourced labels, and on Meta-World drawer-open and plate-slide with synthetic and blind human labels, harder MPPI search cuts true return by up to 76% while held-out label accuracy stays at 0.75-0.97; with human labels the drawer opens in 0 of 20 runs, against 10 of 10 for the cloned policy the planner starts from. The effect persists with a learned dynamics model and an image scorer. We prove that $\chi^2$-regularized MPPI at a temperature set by the scorer's error spread on the proposals is worst-case optimal, and that no gain can be certified once that spread exceeds the scorer's own. Calibrated from 100 ranked proposal pairs, this rule is the safest fix we test, keeping 86-94% of the cloned policy's return on drawer-open and plate-slide.

9e9f15d38d433e570d1e8a30.excerpt: arXiv:2611.14808v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Advances in large language models (LLMs) are enabling software-as-a-service (SaaS) providers to automate longer business workflows with agents. In subscription-based SaaS deployments, model and tool calls consume provider resources without additional customer payments. Because the agent autonomously decides when to stop, a malicious tenant can send a prompt to the agent, exploiting its completion decisions to extend execution and waste provider resources. In this paper, we present OverServe, a multi-agent framework for constructing such attacks against SaaS agents. OverServe co-designs Model Context Protocol (MCP) status tools and completion-confirmation prompts for the attacker. Each tool call returns accurate status and terminates normally, yet the agent may repeatedly check an unfinished condition to satisfy the prompt. This consumes the SaaS provider's resources even after the original business task is completed. OverServe constructs service-specific tool--prompt pairs and uses separate tool and prompt reviews to guide candidate pair selection. Tested tool specifications trigger no alerts in the evaluated MCP scanners. We evaluate Qwen, Nemotron, DeepSeek, and Sonnet on selected tasks from nine benchmarks. All OverServe runs pass the original task checks. OverServe can reach a maximal amplification of API requests by $93.88\times$ while preserving the original task goal and collateral checks.

8056e1e8b9532b688d3f2899.title_original: 엔진엑스(NGINX), 원격 코드 실행 가능한 ‘NGINX2Root’ 취약점(CVE-2026-123007 외 5건) 긴급 업데이트 권고
8056e1e8b9532b688d3f2899.excerpt: 생성형 AI 제작 이미지 F5가 웹 서버 소프트웨어 NGINX(엔진엑스)에서 발견된 원격 코드 실행 취약점 5건(CVE-2026-123007 등, 일명 NGINX2Root)에 대한 보안 업데이트를 배포했습니다. 이번 취약점은 NGINX의 HTTP/2·HTTP/3 처리 모듈, 이름 확인(resolver) 기능, 메일 프록시 모듈에서 발생하는 메모리 손상 결함으로, 인증 없이 원격에서 조작된 요청을 보내 NGINX 작업 프로세스(worker)를 중단시키거나, 메모리 주소 무작위화(ASLR)가 꺼져 있거나 우회되는 환경에서는 임의 코드를 실행할 수 있습니다. F5는 5건 모두 CVSS 4.0 기준 9.2점(Critical), CVSS 3.1 기준 8.1점(High)으로 평가했으며, 한국인터넷진흥원(KISA)도 보안 업데이트 권고를 발표했습니다. 취약점을 발견한 보안업체 Xint는 대표 취약점(CVE-2026-123007)으로 클라우드 서버를 원격 공격해 명령 실행에 성공했고, 별도의 리눅스 커널 취약점과 연계해 루트 권한까지 획득했다고 밝혔습니다. NGINX는 웹 서버, 리버스 프록시, 로드밸런서, 쿠버네티스 인그레스 등 외부 요청이 가장 먼저 도달하는 위치에서 널리 쓰이는 만큼, 운영자분들은 아래 내용을 참고해 신속하게 보안 업데이트를 적용하시기 바랍니다. 취약점 개요 CVE CVE-2026-123007, CVE-2026-123634, CVE-2026-123633, CVE-2026-121810, CVE-2026-113425 (일명 NGINX2Root) 영향 컴포넌트 NGINX Plus, NGINX Open Source 및 이를 포함한 F5 NGINX 제품 ngx_http_v2_module , ngx_http_v3_module , NGINX resolver, ngx_mail_proxy_module 취약점 유형 정수 언더플로로 인한 힙 버퍼 오버플로(1건), 해제된 메모리 사용(Use After Free, 4건) 작업 프로세스 중단(서비스 거부), 메모리 손상, 원격 코드 실행 가능 공격 조건 네트워크, 인증 불필요, 사용자 개입 불필요, 공격 복잡도 높음 취약점별로 HTTP/2·HTTP/3 사용, 메일 프록시 사용 등 특정 설정에서만 해당 심각도 Critical (CVSS v4.0 9.2) / High (CVSS v3.1 8.1) - F5 평가 (5건 동일) CVSS:4.0/AV:N/AC:H/AT:N/PR:N/UI:N/VC:H/VI:H/VA:H/SC:N/SI:N/SA:N 영향 대상 NGINX Open Source 1.30.6 이하, 1.31.0 ~ 1.31.8 NGINX Plus 37.0.0 ~ 37.2.0.1 및 R34 ~ R36 공개일 2026. 11. 18. 7c62bcc10ac6af3e22878207.title_original: PSA: Critical NGINX HTTP/2 Vulnerabilities: What WordPress Site Owners Should Know
7c62bcc10ac6af3e22878207.excerpt: NGINX has released fixes for two critical HTTP/2 vulnerabilities, CVE-2026-123007 and CVE-2026-123633 . Both can lead to remote code execution on affected servers. If your WordPress site uses NGINX, keep an eye out for guidance from your hosting provider about whether its servers are affected and patched. NGINX lists versions 1.9.5–1.30.6 and 1.31.0–1.31.8 as affected by CVE-2026-123007; CVE-2026-123633 starts at 1.19.7 . Fixed open-source versions 1.30.7 (stable) and 1.31.9 (mainline) were released November 18, 2026. Both flaws require NGINX to accept client HTTP/2. CVE-2026-123633 also requires forwarding requests to a backend while a worker runs low on connections. HTTP/2 is off unless a server’s configuration enables it. NGINX’s source build omits the HTTP/2 module by default , but NGINX’s own prebuilt packages include it , and hosting configurations vary. Why This Is Important for WordPress Sites NGINX can serve a WordPress site or sit in front of its application server. It handles HTTP/2 before requests reach PHP or WordPress. Successful exploitation could run code with the NGINX worker’s privileges, putting sites and data on that server at risk. Updating WordPress, plugins, themes, or Wordfence will not patch NGINX. The Wordfence firewall runs at the PHP application layer . Your host or server administrator must install the server fix; a Wordfence scan cannot confirm its patch status.
