Binding is our means of verifying whether a system is vulnerable to a given attack: from a bound pattern we derive an attacker model, turn its effect into a temporal-logic property, and check that property against the system with and without a countermeasure, reporting the control that defeats the attack. We describe the signature, schemas, profiles for approach, and explore how CAPEC can support reasoning about robotics security.

de9461d3e3b5cf1e52eafb77.title_original: Exploited Before It Was Fixed? Vulnerability Timelines from Open, Machine-Readable Evidence
de9461d3e3b5cf1e52eafb77.excerpt: arXiv:2611.22479v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: -05-X-03), Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalogs, and exploitation sightings. We introduce an evidence model implemented in Vulnerability-Lookup that selects the earliest evidence for each lifecycle event, distinguishes vulnerability-specific records, preserves date precision, and ensures traceability to original sources. Among 3,758 vulnerability identifiers with exploitation evidence, 98% have disclosure dates, while only 15.7% have patch evidence. Vendor-side dates required by VTEM are entirely absent. Most exploitation dates originate from catalog listings, including 1,041 entries associated with bulk catalog imports. After excluding these entries and ambiguous same-day observations, 59 vulnerabilities exhibit patch evidence following exploitation evidence, with a median interval of 7.6 days, predominantly between catalog listings and distributor fixes. Evidence traceability also exposes systematic measurement errors: one collector incorrectly classified exploit publications as active exploitation, accounting for 40% of initial exploitation dates, while another catalog assigned vulnerability publication timestamps to 11% of its listings. Our findings demonstrate that exploitation-to-patch intervals are computationally measurable, but their reliability depends on the availability, precision, and provenance of published evidence. We identify the additional disclosure, exploitation observation, and patch availability timestamps needed to improve vulnerability lifecycle measurements.

ecb1aa84cd4c4f5857c8aae1.title_original: How Well Is My Artwork Protected? Predicting and Tailoring Protection against Style Mimicry by Personalization
ecb1aa84cd4c4f5857c8aae1.excerpt: arXiv:2611.22486v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Protection tools add an imperceptible perturbation to each artwork so that a model personalized on it fails to imitate its style, and they apply one recipe, a protection method at a fixed strength, to every artwork. We find that the same recipe protects artworks very differently, well beyond the noise of personalization seeds, and that cheap signals predict this protection before any personalization. Because protection rises and falls together across recipes, our method, Patina, predicts the protection of every recipe from one short trial protection and gives each artwork the weakest recipe whose predicted protection reaches a chosen level. At the same level of visibility, Patina lets more artworks pass the protection threshold than any single recipe and warns the artist about artworks for which no recipe is predicted to pass it.

9093103f84e1155e99a05cb4.title_original: Flexibility Has a Price: Quantifying Modality Policies in Maliciously Secure Multi-Biometric Authentication
9093103f84e1155e99a05cb4.excerpt: arXiv:2611.22714v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Multi-biometric authentication improves robustness and accessibility by combining information from multiple biometric modalities. Existing research has primarily focused on secure multimodal authentication, feature fusion, and recognition performance, while paying comparatively little attention to the security implications of modality-flexible authentication policies. At the same time, most systems provide limited cryptographic protection for biometric data during authentication. This paper addresses both challenges. We first study modality flexibility as a security decision rather than merely a usability feature. Each accepted modality subset creates an authentication entry point, and the resulting risk depends on the joint behavior of all accepted subsets and the attempt budget. We introduce a framework for quantifying this security cost and develop a policy-selection procedure that identifies policies satisfying a target risk level while supporting users who can present only a subset of modalities. We then present SUPERMBA, a two-server privacy-preserving authentication system that enforces the selected policy without revealing biometric templates or the modality subset used in an authentication attempt. The protocol provides verifiable policy enforcement even when one server is malicious and executes the same computation irrespective of the chosen policy or modality subset. Experiments on the three-modality MULB+ dataset show that allowing all modality subsets increases impostor risk from 1.21% for the weakest entry to 4.42% for the union of entries. On VidTIMIT, the increase is substantially smaller and is not statistically resolved with the available identities. SUPERMBA completes an authentication attempt in only 6.42 ms on MULB+ and 6.03 ms on VidTIMIT.

f41a831739a77ddeded5e835.title_original: Provable Mixing Properties of Parallel Mixnets Revisited
f41a831739a77ddeded5e835.excerpt: arXiv:2611.22732v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A mix-network (mixnet) is a routing network that breaks source-to-destination message trackability by indistinguishably mixing the routes of concurrently transmitted messages, thus providing anonymity to senders, receivers and sender-receiver pairs. Given their potential use in high-stakes scenarios like protecting whistleblowers, one would like to prove formally that sender anonymity holds in a mixnet, even against strong adversaries that can compromise subsets of mixnet servers. However, existing work on anonymity in mixnets is either limited to linear mixnets (which do not scale horizontally), relies on special provisions such as additional noise or chaff messages, or is empirical -- typically based on entropy, which does not provide strong guarantees if the adversary has auxiliary information. In this paper, we present a new analysis of parallel mixnets which scale horizontally, showing that these networks can provide strong indistinguishability for messages even without additional noise messages. Our analysis works by bounding the statistical variance of the adversary's posterior likelihood of where a message of interest is at a given point in time. Using concentration bounds on this distribution, we show that parallel mixnets satisfy $(\varepsilon, \delta)$-differential indistinguishability for messages routed through the mixnet (similar to $(\varepsilon, \delta)$-differential privacy) with very small failure probabilities $\delta$ and small privacy parameters $\varepsilon$ under reasonable operating conditions. Our model also enables an examination of the quantitative trade-off between anonymity, latency and per-router bandwidth in parallel mixnets.

2f5bc5db71bd36b1b5bf2081.title_original: Guarded Swarms in the Loop: A ROS 2/PX4 Digital Twin for Hybrid Digital-Analog Coordination of UAV/UGV Swarms
2f5bc5db71bd36b1b5bf2081.excerpt: arXiv:2611.22773v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Swarms of unmanned aerial and ground vehicles (UAV/UGV) operating in contested environments cannot rely on software alone for physical safety, since the software stack and its networks are part of the attack surface. The Guarded Swarms architecture addresses this by pairing a digital coordination layer, built on Topic-Based Communication Space Petri Nets (TB-CSPN), with an independent analog safety layer that can veto unsafe actuation commands. So far, the architecture has been specified and argued for, but not executed. We present the first executable instantiation of Guarded Swarms as a digital twin built on ROS 2, the PX4 autopilot in software-in-the-loop mode, and Gazebo, with two UAVs and one UGV in a coastal counter-UAS scenario. The TB-CSPN transition chain, from multi-modal sensing through human authorization to vehicle tasking, is mapped one-to-one onto ROS 2 nodes, and the analog layer is modeled as a per-vehicle Virtual Safety Board that gates every command. Eight groups of experiments show that the three negative guarantees of the architecture (no mission from conflicting, temporally incoherent, or unauthorized evidence) hold at three distinct stages of the chain in all 60 counterfactual runs; that threat confirmation is bounded by the narrowest sensing modality; that the safety layer exercises its full modeled envelope independently of the coordination layer; and, under fault injection, that it prevents every collision caused by a forged mission or a compromised worker once its veto is enforced by an independent gate, whereas a veto left to the compromised worker prevents none. The twin also exposes implementation-level hazards that the architectural specification does not address, and it draws an explicit line between the properties that simulation can validate and those that only hardware can.

92810be3a3dbb1d8fab943d4.title_original: CaFe: Causally Faithful Conditional Traffic Scenario Generation
92810be3a3dbb1d8fab943d4.excerpt: arXiv:2611.22855v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Language-conditioned traffic simulation enables scalable test scenarios steered by natural language. The goal is to control selected agents while surrounding traffic reacts to their observed behaviour. For example, a vehicle instructed to cut in late should cause the following vehicle to brake only when the manoeuvre becomes observable. Yet simulators can leak private instructions across agents, causing surrounding vehicles to react before the instructed behaviour becomes observable. Such premature reactions defuse desired events and alter the ensuing closed-loop scenario. Existing benchmarks measure what agents do, not what they could have known, leaving this failure unmeasured. We formalise it as intent leakage and address it through evaluation, data and modelling. Our paired intervention test holds an instructed agent's executed trajectory fixed while varying its private instruction, isolating leakage-induced changes in surrounding agents. We also construct WOMD-PACT, an automatically generated, verifiable dataset of 531,099 WOMD scenes with timed behaviour tags with reaction episodes identified through a counterfactual ghost test and grounded private instructions. Finally, we introduce CaFe, a dual-stream diffusion-forcing simulator fine-tuned in closed loop that restricts inter-agent interactions to public beliefs, preserving legitimate anticipation without leaking private intent. Our evaluation reveals that existing conditioning designs displace 23-83% of nearby uninstructed agents through private-intent leakage, even when the instructed agent's executed motion is held fixed. CaFe eliminates measurable leakage while maintaining comparable WOSAC realism (0.763), demonstrating that causal faithfulness can be enforced without sacrificing measured simulation realism.

957b6f3d25686b91b914cd19.title_original: Can Verifiable PIR Match the Online Efficiency of SimplePIR?
957b6f3d25686b91b914cd19.excerpt: arXiv:2611.22911v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Verifiable Private Information Retrieval (vPIR) ensures that a malicious server cannot return tampered database records, but it traditionally incurs significant overhead compared to classical PIR.Recent advancements, notably VeriSimplePIR, approach the online efficiency of SimplePIR by introducing a proof preprocessing phase and requiring only lightweight client-side online verification. However, this scheme relies on an additional Short Integer Solution (SIS) assumption and SIS-based commitments, which only support relaxed range proofs. Consequently, these schemes are forced to adopt significantly weaker parameter choices, resulting in additional online overhead. In this paper, we propose a novel vPIR protocol that employs a newly designed error-correcting code-based commitment scheme as the database digest. This approach (i)supports efficient proofs of linear relations, (ii) achieves precise range proofs and (iii) eliminates the reliance on the SIS assumption. Thus, our scheme successfully adopts parameter choices identical to those of SimplePIR. As a result, our vPIR protocol is the first to achieve exactly the same online communication and server computation costs as SimplePIR, while keeping online client computation nearly identical. Additionally, compared to VeriSimplePIR,our protocol reduces online communication and client-side computation by approximately 20%, and decreases online server-side computation by over 35%.

d52494b4fdf879209a826a3d.title_original: On Improving the Adoption, Usability, and Retention of Static Application Security Testing (SAST) Tools
d52494b4fdf879209a826a3d.excerpt: arXiv:2611.21621v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: As the Internet connects more of the world, software vulnerabilities create growing security risks. Because software developers are responsible for building and maintaining secure applications, they rely on tools and techniques that help identify vulnerabilities early in development. Static Application Security Testing (SAST) tools analyze source code to identify potential security weaknesses before software is deployed. Although SAST can help developers address vulnerabilities proactively, these tools also present usability and adoption challenges. This thesis examines those challenges and explores ways to improve the adoption, usability, and continued use of SAST. First, a literature review of 89 research works related to SAST implementation and continued usage identifies recurring developer concerns, including false positives and other usability barriers that can reduce trust in SAST results. Second, the thesis presents a process for automating the execution of SAST tools and formatting their output so that findings are more meaningful and actionable to developers. A real-world use case evaluates an implementation of this process and gathers developer feedback. Participants reported satisfaction with several aspects of the process and indicated that it increased their willingness to use the SAST tool.

4a3295d3d71e9aea125ae862.title_original: Wrong Input, Wrong Threshold: Re-evaluating Adversarial Facial Privacy
4a3295d3d71e9aea125ae862.excerpt: arXiv:2611.21923v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Published face-privacy methods report protection above 90% against black-box recognition models. That number comes from an evaluation protocol with two independent defects, reported in a measure that cannot size either one. The input is wrong: methods published since 2022 feed the network the whole photograph, or a detector's box, where deployed systems detect, align to a landmark template and crop. Re-scoring the same files through a realistic front end costs a standard transfer attack 56% of its dodging protection and a budget-allocating attack 7%, with no image regenerated. The measure is wrong: that loss is a difference of success rates, so it saturates, moving by 8.2x over a budget sweep while the effect beneath it moves by 1.34x. We therefore report the paired cosine shift, in which both thresholds cancel algebraically, so the input defect holds without committing to a calibration. Measured that way it is 2.2x and 10.7x larger on three unseen recognizers, and at matched budget it reverses the L-infinity transfer ranking: the one surveyed method that aligns at evaluation gains 0.18 where MI-FGSM loses 0.05. The cause is a resampling mismatch, not perturbation lost outside the crop; optimising through a differentiable alignment operator largely removes it, adding +24 to +58 points on unseen recognizers and a commercial system, with a residual on one of them. The thresholds are wrong: the four constants inherited since 2021 hold the false-accept rate near its nominal 1% on aligned crops but admit 2.3-5.4% on whole images, with an opposite-signed bias across dodging and impersonation, the two tasks reported side by side. Differentiable alignment and gallery scoring are not new: the first generation of this literature used both, and we show what dropping them cost.

df088a1de53476fc0fa0575a.title_original: GuardAgent: A Memory-Augmented Agentic Framework for Adaptive Detection of Adversarial Promotions in LLM-Based Recommendation
df088a1de53476fc0fa0575a.excerpt: arXiv:2611.22274v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: In traditional recommender systems (RSs), textual information typically serves as auxiliary signals for representation learning. In contrast, in LLM-based RSs, textual information becomes the primary medium for recommendation generation through semantic understanding and reasoning. This shift fundamentally changes the attack surface, making promotion-driven manipulations more feasible, effective, and harder to detect. However, effectively detecting such attacks remains largely unexplored. To fill this gap, we present the first systematic study on detecting promotion-driven attacks against LLM-based RSs, aiming to safeguard next-generation recommendation platforms. Specifically, we propose GuardAgent, a novel LLM-powered agentic detection framework that operates through a loop of Perception, Action, Reflection and Memory. In contrast to conventional LLM-based detectors that function in a static, one-off, and opaque fashion, GuardAgent continually learns and self-evolves to adapt to unseen threat patterns while generating explainable reasoning traces and outcomes. Extensive experiments on real-world datasets demonstrate that GuardAgent achieves state-of-the-art generalization performance, laying the foundation for robust and trustworthy recommendation in practical settings.

9af096bcacb162d8936d1712.title_original: A Little Advice Suffices: Diffie-Hellman Is as Hard as Discrete Logarithm
9af096bcacb162d8936d1712.excerpt: arXiv:2611.22290v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Is computing a Diffie-Hellman key as hard as computing a discrete logarithm? Maurer showed that it is, given a few bits of advice, provided that short intervals contain enough integers with only small prime factors; that proviso has stood for thirty years. We remove it. For every prime $p$ there is an advice string of $O(\log p)$ bits, depending only on $p$, with which discrete logarithms in every group of order $p$ are computed in polynomial time from a Diffie-Hellman oracle. The reduction is the classical one; what was missing was a proof that short intervals contain polylogarithmically smooth integers. We show that a zero-free half-plane for the Riemann zeta function, which is now known, gives the expected number of $(\log x)^K$-smooth integers in every interval $[x,x+x^\theta]$ with $\theta>17/30$. With smoothness this small the saddle point of the counting integral lies just to the left of the line $\mathrm{Re}\,s=1$, and a zero-free strip of any fixed width absorbs the shift once $K$ is large. Genus-2 Jacobians, whose orders fill such intervals, then turn one of these integers into the order of an auxiliary group. The same input removes the smoothness assumption from Maurer and Raub's impossibility of field-homomorphic one-way permutations and from the yes/no-query reduction of Koblitz, Menezes and Shparlinski. It also makes Wolf's characterisation unconditional: discrete logarithm and Diffie-Hellman are generically equivalent exactly when the group order has no large repeated prime factor.

ed7d35e36bba6df9b129ce93.title_original: Fast and Strong Image Protection against Diffusion Personalization
ed7d35e36bba6df9b129ce93.excerpt: arXiv:2611.22494v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Personalized text-to-image diffusion models can reproduce a person from a handful of photographs. Image protection perturbs each image before publication so that fine-tuning on it fails, but it optimizes every perturbation from scratch, so its cost grows with the number of images. We present the protective diffusion model (PDM), which is trained once and samples the perturbation of a new image over many denoising steps. PDM distills an iterative teacher and is then post-trained with the target residual projection (TRP) loss as a reward, a stronger objective than existing ones. PDM outperforms nine baselines on faces and artworks and nearly matches its teacher at a tenth of the cost.

950ba0d8bf614a5f1148fb94.title_original: Missing Security-Fix Backporting for GitHub Actions Workflows
950ba0d8bf614a5f1148fb94.excerpt: arXiv:2611.22519v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: GitHub natively supports workflow automation through GitHub Actions, now the dominant CI/CD tool on the platform. Yet keeping these workflows secure remains an ongoing burden: maintainers often patch a vulnerability on the default branch but leave the same flaw on the release and maintenance branches that downstream consumers continue to build from. Carrying a known fix onto these divergent branches, called backporting, is rarely done, and this paper presents the first large-scale empirical study quantifying the resulting gap. From a public corpus of GitHub Actions workflow histories, we mine 1,903,191 workflow-modifying commits, scan each before and after with the static scanner zizmor to identify 69,865 security fixes across 24,238 projects, and audit every release branch to check whether each fix was carried over. The gap is pervasive: 224,392 of 474,490 audited release branches remain vulnerable, and deliberate backporting is rare and slow, with only 19,476 of 78,907 already-fixed branches confirmed as plausible backports at a median lag of 243 days. We thus design WorkflowBP, the first technique for automated security-fix backporting of GitHub Actions workflows. WorkflowBP takes a neuro-symbolic approach: it compiles a default-branch fix into a domain-specific representation called the Workflow Semantic Patch (WSP) and applies it to each divergent branch by matching jobs and steps based on their content rather than their position, while an LLM synthesizes the WSP for the most divergent cases the deterministic engine cannot resolve. On 12,000 real unpatched workflow files from our study, WorkflowBP produces a scanner-checked backport for 67.9%. We further submit 176 issues with WorkflowBP-generated backports to real-world projects, 44 of which have been confirmed or fixed by developers.

ffa48ba2eda9d315fef36e5b.title_original: Propose with the Gradient, Accept with the Loss: One Hedged Attack for Pixel-Sparse Robustness
ffa48ba2eda9d315fef36e5b.excerpt: arXiv:2611.22596v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: A pixel-sparse adversary may change a few pixels of an image to any value. Robustness to such attacks is currently measured with an ensemble, sparse-AutoAttack (sAA), because its members fail in different places: sparse projected gradient descent (sPGD) trusts a first-order model that a full pixel change breaks, and sparse random search (Sparse-RS) ignores the gradient even where it is informative. We show that both attacks are local searches, each a proposal distribution plus an acceptance rule, and ask what such a search can learn from the gradient. A Taylor bound says what to measure, and measurements at the states the search visits give five rules. The sign of the gradient is its most reliable use at a single pixel and sets a new pixel's value. Its ranking of candidate pixels should be followed loosely, and its ranking of the pixels to remove, which is often more reliable, can be followed more closely. A pixel should not be proposed twice before a move is accepted, and acceptance should be decided by the loss alone. These rules define Gradient-guided Random Search (GRS), which runs once and costs one forward and one backward pass per step. On 13 CIFAR-10 configurations and 5 ImageNet models, GRS matches or beats the best single member of sAA and is within one point of sAA itself or stronger on 17 of 18 settings, and it is significantly stronger than sAA on 8. It uses 3 instead of up to 7 forward-pass units, and on CIFAR-10 it runs 3.7 to 5.0 times faster than the members of sAA run in full.

a1bc8d1ad8135e1c7e13e9d8.title_original: Who Pays for Byzantine Robustness? Validity, Data-Share Dictatorships, and Fairness When Only a Few Hospitals Collaborate
a1bc8d1ad8135e1c7e13e9d8.excerpt: arXiv:2611.22904v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Clinical federated learning (FL) collaborations typically connect only three to six hospitals, yet Byzantine-robust aggregation rules are designed and benchmarked on synthetic partitions across dozens of equal-sized clients. We conduct an empirical audit of eight standard aggregation rules: FedAvg, coordinate-wise median, trimmed mean, Krum, Multi-Krum, Bulyan, geometric median (GeoMed), and Centered Clipping (CC). We evaluate both unweighted and sample-size-weighted variants across three cross-silo medical datasets from the FLamby benchmark: Fed-Heart-Disease ($n = 4$ hospitals), Fed-TCGA-BRCA ($n = 6$ regions), and Fed-ISIC2019 ($n = 6$ centres). We execute 54,214 training runs across enumerated attacker coalitions ($f \in \{1, 2\}$) paired with exact-twin leave-out controls that decompose performance drops into honest data loss versus adversarial attack damage. We report three findings. First, client-count validity checks fail to capture breakdown in skewed medical consortia: while $n = 6, f = 1$ satisfies every count condition except Bulyan's, assigning sample-size weights turns median and GeoMed into a clean-model dictatorship whenever a single hospital holds more than half the training data, and causes weighted median, GeoMed, and CC to collapse when that dominant centre attacks. Second, exact-twin leave-out controls reveal that when the largest hospital attacks, the apparent failure of count-based robust rules is predominantly caused by the loss of honest training data (7.5 to 10.4 points on ISIC) rather than adversarial perturbation (2.3 to 3.8 points on ISIC). Conversely, weight-dependent rules suffer large true attack damage (16.1 to 25.1 points on ISIC). Third, unweighted robust rules consistently discount whichever institution generates the most atypical parameter updates, penalizing the smallest hospital on Heart but penalizing larger institutions on TCGA and ISIC.

22a1b0ea104cabc549569431.title_original: Dissecting the GPU Load/Store Unit and Exposing Its Security Risks
22a1b0ea104cabc549569431.excerpt: arXiv:2611.23022v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: GPUs are the main platform for large-scale machine learning and power the largest supercomputers. Their load/store units (LSUs) often determine kernel performance and have been exploited in prior attacks. Yet what is known about the LSU is only a few isolated mechanisms and parameters, and even a single one has been enough for an attack. In particular, it is still unknown what a load costs, where loads contend, and even whether a warp can starve due to contention. Until each is measured, neither its security risk nor a defense is known. We reverse-engineer how the LSU serves load instructions on recent NVIDIA GPUs with microbenchmarks and analyze the security implications. We give a cycle-accurate latency formula for a global L1 hit or shared memory access from the addresses it touches, whose address-dependent terms are bank conflicts and the L1 tag lookup; we show that loads contend at both, and that when the LSU pipeline is full a warp can starve a warp of a later-launched block. We then show that the LSU's attack surface is far broader than prior attacks revealed: through channels never exploited before, it can leak information, communicate covertly, and degrade colocated workloads. Through either global bank conflicts or tag lookups alone, we recover a full AES-128 key under the threat model of prior GPU AES timing attacks. Under NVIDIA's Multi-Process Service (MPS), the bank access and the tag lookup each open a covert channel across processes, whose rate rises with each GPU generation. Also under MPS, this starvation lets one warp slow a colocated cuBLAS matrix multiplication by up to 750x on the A100 and 563x on the H100.

79cce814d2426bea4dc52ae7.title_original: Distortion-Free Semantic Watermarks for Black-Box Generative Models
79cce814d2426bea4dc52ae7.excerpt: arXiv:2611.23208v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We present a provably distortion-free semantic watermarking algorithm that requires only black-box sampling access to a generative model and black-box access to a semantic embedding. A watermark is called distortion-free if, averaged over its secret detection key, it leaves the generator's output distribution unchanged; this provides a formal guarantee that watermarking does not reduce output quality. Conventional such watermarks are often brittle to transformations. This is especially problematic for images, where benign operations such as compression, cropping, or resizing change the entire pixel representation. Semantic watermarks therefore require detection to be robust to content-preserving transformations. Previous methods combining these properties rely heavily on specific white-box properties of the underlying model: either to autoregressive text generation or to diffusion-specific access, such as control of the initial noise or diffusion inversion. In contrast, our construction is fully generic: It only interacts with the generative model and the semantic embedding, a function that determines the notion of "preserving content" under which detection should be robust, via sample and query access. We then instantiate this framework for image generation. We characterize the two competing properties required of the semantic embedding: it should remain stable under transformations that preserve an image's content, but should distinguish independent generations from the same prompt. We train an image encoder directly for this tradeoff. The resulting encoder improves separation while maintaining stability over off-the-shelf alternatives and enables strong aggregate detection while remaining robust to various transformations. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our watermark scheme on both open-source and closed models, which is possible only due to restriction to black-box access.

544c3fad2ed8892113f301ec.title_original: HE-LRM: Encrypted Deep Learning Recommendation Models using Fully Homomorphic Encryption
544c3fad2ed8892113f301ec.excerpt: arXiv:2506.18150v5 Announce Type: replace Abstract: FHE inference systems primarily target models with dense inputs, while Deep Learning Recommendation Models (DLRMs) contain sparse categorical features that require lookups into embedding tables. Encrypted lookups are challenging because indexing is not natively supported and must be expressed using SIMD arithmetic. A direct one-hot formulation does not scale. Prior work addresses parts of this problem through embedding compression or compact encrypted queries. However, it does not address complete DLRM inference, leaving open how private lookup interacts with downstream computation and memory constraints. We present HE-LRM, the first end-to-end FHE system for private DLRM inference. We use deterministic compositional embedding compression with client-side digit decomposition, avoiding expensive homomorphic selector construction while consuming only one multiplicative level. We further develop a block-diagonal packing strategy that performs lookups across multiple embedding tables using optimized BSGS linear transformations and produces encrypted embeddings directly compatible with downstream inference. We extend Orion with a high-performance GPU backend and achieve 9 ms for single-inference embedding lookup. We also show that GPU memory capacity limits batching and therefore the latency-bound throughput in such systems. On Criteo, HE-LRM achieves complete encrypted inference with server-side latencies of 154-247 ms on a single GPU. We open-source HE-LRM at https://github.com/baahl-nyu/orion

4aa15cfb72fec11288778a4d.title_original: PSM: Prompt Sensitivity Minimization via LLM-Guided Black-Box Optimization
4aa15cfb72fec11288778a4d.excerpt: arXiv:2511.16209v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: System prompts are critical for guiding the behavior of Large Language Models (LLMs), yet they often contain proprietary logic or sensitive information, making them a prime target for extraction attacks. Adversarial queries can successfully elicit these hidden instructions, posing significant security and privacy risks. Existing defense mechanisms frequently rely on heuristics, incur substantial computational overhead, or are inapplicable to models accessed via black-box APIs. This paper introduces a novel framework for hardening system prompts through shield appending, a lightweight approach that adds a protective textual layer to the original prompt. Our core contribution is the formalization of prompt hardening as a utility-constrained optimization problem. We leverage an LLM-as-optimizer to search the space of possible SHIELDs, seeking to minimize a leakage metric derived from a suite of adversarial attacks, while simultaneously preserving task utility above a specified threshold, measured by semantic fidelity to baseline outputs. This black-box, optimization-driven methodology is lightweight and practical, requiring only API access to the target and optimizer LLMs. We demonstrate empirically that our optimized SHIELDs significantly reduce prompt leakage against a comprehensive set of extraction attacks, outperforming established baseline defenses without compromising the model's intended functionality. Our work presents a paradigm for developing robust, utility-aware defenses in the escalating landscape of LLM security. The code is made public on the following link: https://github.com/psm-defense/psm

00977a48d8bade8862b6f93e.title_original: IH-Benchmark: A Conflict-Centered Benchmark for Instruction-Hierarchy Robustness in Large Language Models
00977a48d8bade8862b6f93e.excerpt: arXiv:2607.25987v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: When a language model receives conflicting instructions from different priority levels, which one does it actually follow? This question lies at the heart of reliable LLM deployment. Existing benchmarks answer this only partially, often focusing on a single hierarchy component or adapting public datasets with limited tool-use coverage. We present IH-Benchmark, a conflict-centered benchmark for instruction-hierarchy robustness across direct System $\succ$ User (S $\succ$ U) conflicts and tool-mediated User $\succ$ Tool (U $\succ$ T) conflicts. We organize tests into seven constraint categories according to the higher-priority requirements under evaluation. Each test is evaluated with a uniform binary pass/fail protocol combining a predicate domain-specific language (DSL) with rubric-based LLM judges. We report category-balanced compliance rates and evaluate non-conflict controls separately. Our evaluation of 32 model configurations over five runs each reveals substantial variation in overall compliance, with scores ranging from 32.9% to 97.8%. Models achieve higher compliance on S $\succ$ U than on U $\succ$ T on average, at 84.6% and 69.6%, respectively. Strong performance on the former track does not guarantee comparable robustness on the latter. Constraint hardening provides a prompt-based defense, but its benefits depend on the model and how conflicting instructions are delivered. Several models also resist unauthorized tool actions more reliably than injected instructions that alter response language or factual content. Together, these results show that high aggregate compliance can conceal weaknesses in specific conflict tracks and instruction requirements. We release IH-Benchmark, including the benchmark corpus, agent simulators, and evaluation harness, at LINK_RELEASE_AFTER_PEER_REVIEW.

88f382e61f19204f1ee57d31.title_original: A Deployment-Oriented and Resource-Efficient Neuro-Symbolic Framework for Explainable DDoS Detection in Operational Technology Networks
88f382e61f19204f1ee57d31.excerpt: arXiv:2608.16769v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: This paper presents a hybrid neural-symbolic detector of distributed denial-of-service (DDoS) attacks on the availability of operational technology (OT) networks, designed for their resource-constrained gateways, and an evaluation matched to deployment. A compact gated recurrent unit (GRU) is fused at score level with a shallow, readable decision tree, and weight and threshold are selected on validation data under an explicit false-positive budget, whose attainment in finite samples is analysed. The evaluation on CIC-DDoS2019, Edge-IIoTset and CICIoT23 uses contiguous or capture-held-out partitions, dependence-aware intervals, and precision and alert load at operational prevalence. Over ten seeds at a 1% budget, the hybrid's false-negative rate on CIC-DDoS2019 is 0.08%, against 0.26% for the GRU and 0.17% for the tree. With a day of mostly unseen attack families held out, the tree alone carries the decision. Audits bound these claims: Edge-IIoTset is saturated by duplicates, no benchmark as used provides interleaved traffic in capture order, and an unconstrained tree is more accurate on two of them, so the case for the hybrid rests on short, stable rules and a measured footprint. On a Siemens SIMATIC IoT2050 gateway, tested with Modbus/TCP and MQTT floods, the INT8 model needs 2.9 ms per window, 31 MB of memory and 3.5 mJ per inference.

49e5b9b811e4fbed9938b650.title_original: IoMT-SecAlarmBench: A Semi-Synthetic Counterfactual Benchmark for Integrity Attacks in IoMT
49e5b9b811e4fbed9938b650.excerpt: arXiv:2608.26416v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The Internet of Medical Things (IoMT) combines clinical physiological data with cyber-system information, creating challenges in determining whether an abnormal reading reflects a genuine physiological event, a device fault, or a cyber-attack within the expected physiological range. Answering this requires counterfactual ground truth, which no existing dataset provides. We present IoMT-SecAlarmBench, a semi-synthetic benchmark that injects controlled integrity attacks into genuine coupled ECG+PPG recordings using a structured experimental design combining four attack morphologies, four severity levels, two physiological plausibility conditions, and replay attacks. Each injected window retains its cause, attack subtype, and the clean signal that would have been observed without the attack. We evaluate six detectors from five method families using threshold-independent measures and a matched false-alarm budget. Results show no method consistently detects the most difficult cases: replay attacks and low-amplitude transient spikes remain close to chance-level performance across detectors. Results also reveal a trade-off between detecting attacks and distinguishing them from sensor faults: the best-performing detector on hard cases flags fault/artifact windows at 5.3 times its false-alarm rate on normal data. Three-way classification performs poorly for genuine physiological events, and a leakage audit of a dual-modality network dataset indicates previously reported IoMT intrusion-detection performance is partly driven by identifying information. Benchmark, generation code, preprocessing, evaluation tools, and datasheet are released.

2982b0a7bca20a81d48339e6.title_original: rApp/xApp Attestation: A New Security Use Case for O-RAN
2982b0a7bca20a81d48339e6.excerpt: arXiv:2609.24296v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The disaggregation and softwarization introduced by the Open Radio Access Network (O-RAN) architecture enable multi-vendor innovation but also expose the RAN Intelligent Controller (RIC) ecosystem to new runtime security risks. Existing O-RAN specifications define strong safeguards for onboarding, authentication, identity management, and secure communication; however, they do not provide a concrete mechanism for verifying whether deployed rApps and xApps remain in their intended, untampered state during operation. This paper introduces rApp/xApp attestation as a RIC-native O-RAN security use case for runtime integrity verification. Rather than proposing a new cryptographic protocol, the work defines how existing integrity verification techniques can be integrated into O-RAN through attestation modules, attestation agents, RIC application interfaces, and SMO-driven policy coordination. We map the use case to relevant O-RAN Alliance working groups, identify required standardization extensions, and demonstrate feasibility through a lightweight hash-based prototype implemented on the Near-RT RIC platform. Experimental results show attestation latencies below 40 ms across multiple cryptographic hash functions, indicating that runtime attestation can be performed without disrupting time-sensitive RIC operations when appropriately scheduled. Finally, we discuss remaining technical and standardization challenges, including trusted verification, known-good runtime states, scalability, mitigation policies, and future hybrid attestation mechanisms.

50d192290cf241bcf1a17748.excerpt: arXiv:2611.15019v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Encrypted tunnels are widely used to circumvent censorship, which has drawn censors' efforts to detect and block them. As the circumvention tunnels in widest use have largely converged on TLS, detection has shifted from the content of their traffic to its shape, where recent research and real-world blocking events have revealed exploitable fingerprints of tunneling. Existing traffic-shaping obfuscators such as obfs4, however, are fundamentally limited in hiding these fingerprints, as their application-driven design can only add to the shape that the application creates. A schedule-driven obfuscator, which decides when and how much to send independently of the application, can give tunnels any shape but raises new challenges, first and foremost what a good shape is. This paper presents obfsgen, a schedule-driven obfuscator for tunneling traffic. obfsgen samples its schedule from a generative sequence model of normal traffic, which predicts the future shape of a flow from its whole history, to capture the long-range dependencies that make a flow's shape normal. Built around this model, obfsgen addresses system problems that such an obfuscator faces in practice, such as synchronization across a noisy network. We evaluate the (in)distinguishability that obfsgen offers, the performance overhead that it adds and the computational resources that it requires. We see the schedule-driven architecture as the next generation of tunnel obfuscators, and we hope that obfsgen and the rationale behind its design help make such obfuscators practical and deployable.

8759240898661ce9da415901.title_original: CoordX Types: A Trustless, Swappable Type System for Shared Records
8759240898661ce9da415901.excerpt: arXiv:2611.16128v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The CoordX Protocol carries signed and encrypted entries between parties. It proves who wrote each entry and who had permission to write it. It does not say what an entry means. That task belongs above the protocol layer. This paper describes the CoordX type system, the layer that gives entries a meaning. A type is a short document that says how to read one part of a shared record: which entries count, what each position means, what a party may do there, and what a party must do next. The type system has two key properties. It is trustless: a type is an ordinary signed object fixed by its digest, and every party evaluates it for itself over entries that the CoordX Protocol has already verified. No party has to trust a server, a registry or another party's software. It is swappable: a type names the interpreter it is written for, so many interpreters, of different capabilities and designs, can be used side by side in one record. We describe how to write type schemas, and we define the expressive power of the schema language. Payloads form a regular language. Entry structure forms a regular tree language. Every rule and every computed value is a total function in the primitive recursive class, so evaluation always halts. We compare this with KQML, FIPA-ACL and CBCL, and we relate it to language-theoretic security.

8135a3149820ce7612fbeb8b.title_original: RustMC: Automated Verification of Real-World Concurrent Rust
8135a3149820ce7612fbeb8b.excerpt: arXiv:2502.06293v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: RustMC is a stateless model checker that targets push-button verification of unmodified concurrent Rust programs. As both Rust and C/C++ compile to LLVM IR, RustMC builds on GenMC which provides a verification framework for LLVM IR. This allows verification of Rust code and any foreign function dependencies. In this tool paper we present key implementation challenges, use-cases, and an empirical evaluation of RustMC. The challenges include intercepting threading operations, promoting memory intrinsics, and handling uninitialised accesses, all stemming from Rust's unique compilation strategy. Case studies adapted from real-world programs show RustMC finds concurrency bugs in unsafe Rust code, FFI calls to C/C++, and atomic operations. We evaluate our tool's functionality on the Loom model checker test suite and a set of production-level Rust concurrent data structures.

46cb84b31bd472ab28d33b0a.title_original: Visual Contextual Attack: Jailbreaking MLLMs with Image-Driven Context Injection
46cb84b31bd472ab28d33b0a.excerpt: arXiv:2507.02844v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: With the emergence of strong vision language capabilities, multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have demonstrated tremendous potential for real-world applications. However, the security vulnerabilities exhibited by the visual modality pose significant challenges to deploying such models in open-world environments. Recent studies have successfully induced harmful responses from target MLLMs by encoding harmful textual semantics directly into visual inputs. However, in these approaches, the visual modality primarily serves as a trigger for unsafe behavior, often exhibiting semantic ambiguity and lacking grounding in realistic scenarios. In this work, we define a novel setting: vision-centric jailbreak, where visual information serves as a necessary component in constructing a complete and realistic jailbreak context. Building on this setting, we propose the VisCo (Visual Contextual) Attack. VisCo fabricates contextual dialogue using four distinct vision-focused strategies, dynamically generating auxiliary images when necessary to construct a vision-centric jailbreak scenario. To maximize attack effectiveness, it incorporates automatic toxicity obfuscation and semantic refinement to produce a final attack prompt that reliably triggers harmful responses from the target black-box MLLMs. Specifically, VisCo achieves a toxicity score of 4.78 and an Attack Success Rate (ASR) of 85% on MM-SafetyBench against GPT-4o, significantly outperforming the baseline, which achieves a toxicity score of 2.48 and an ASR of 22.2%. Code: https://github.com/Dtc7w3PQ/Visco-Attack.

ebe56384c5905a7e9d0e2eb7.title_original: Angelfish: Leader, DAG, or Anywhere in Between
ebe56384c5905a7e9d0e2eb7.excerpt: arXiv:2509.15847v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: To maximize performance, many modern blockchain systems rely on eventually synchronous, Byzantine fault-tolerant (BFT) consensus protocols. Two protocol designs have emerged in this space: protocols that minimize latency using a leader that drives both data dissemination and consensus, and protocols that maximize throughput using a separate, asynchronous data dissemination layer. Recent protocols such as Partially Synchronous Bullshark and Sailfish combine elements of both approaches by using a DAG to enable parallel data dissemination and a leader that paces DAG formation. This improves latency while achieving state-of-the-art throughput. Yet leader-based protocols still achieve better latency under moderate loads, which are common in practice. We present Angelfish, a hybrid protocol that adapts smoothly across this design space, from leader-based to Sailfish-like DAG-based consensus. Angelfish lets a dynamically adjusted subset of parties use best-effort broadcast to issue lightweight votes instead of reliably broadcasting costlier DAG vertices. This reduces communication, helps lagging nodes catch up, and lowers latency in practice compared to prior DAG-based protocols. Our empirical evaluation shows that Angelfish attains state-of-the-art peak throughput while significantly lowering latency under moderate load, delivering the best of both worlds.

758b93f101267b78c0cd8b9b.title_original: Concave is the New Linear: Sybil Attacks Collapse Anti-Plutocratic DAO Voting
758b93f101267b78c0cd8b9b.excerpt: arXiv:2605.18990v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Decentralized Autonomous Organizations (DAOs) run protocol governance by letting token holders vote on proposals. The dominant rule, voting power proportional to wallet balance, concentrates control among a small number of large holders, fueling the token-control governance attacks that have already compromised real protocols. To counter this concentration, the community has turned to anti-plutocratic voting mechanisms such as Quadratic Voting (QV), which assign sublinear voting power per token with the goal of dampening the influence of large holders. We prove that no voting rule that derives power solely from wallet balance can succeed on a permissionless blockchain. Through a costed model of on-chain voting that captures realistic blockchain frictions -- including per-wallet splitting and voting costs, fixed setup costs, and minimum-balance requirements -- we show that whenever a wallet of any size yields nonzero voting power, a Sybil attacker who splits tokens across many wallets achieves total voting power that grows at least linearly in their token holdings. For concave rules actually proposed to dampen governance power -- those that are positive, increasing, and finite -- we show that the optimal strategy yields power that is asymptotically linear in token holdings, regardless of the cost scheme. Instantiating the model on real DAOs reveals attack costs orders of magnitude below the value at stake. Replaying the ten most recent finalized proposals of five major DAOs (ENS, Compound, Uniswap, Arbitrum, and ZKsync) under linear, quadratic, logarithmic, and power-($\beta = 0.25$) voting, we measure Sybil amplification factors between $1,172\times$ and $4,039\times$ under Quadratic Voting, and exceeding $229,000\times$ under steeper power rules.

2a4120b2a677cee3639a4548.title_original: Tight Lower Bounds for Differentially Private Continual Counting
2a4120b2a677cee3639a4548.excerpt: arXiv:2609.17650v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: The Binary Tree Mechanism is a standard algorithm for differentially private continual counting, but its complete asymptotic optimality under differential privacy has remained unresolved since its introduction. We resolve this question. For $0 \leq \varepsilon \leq 1$, we prove asymptotically tight lower bounds for $\ell_\infty$, mean squared, and maximum per-coordinate expected squared error simultaneously under all regimes of $0 \leq \delta \leq 1/4$. These bounds hold for arbitrary mechanisms, even when the entire stream is available in advance. Our lower bounds match the (blocked) Binary Tree Mechanism instantiated with the best of Laplace or Gaussian noise, establishing its asymptotic optimality. Our proof uses a single hard distribution where elements are ``tagged'' as potentially being the target flipped element via a score evaluated down a tree. A simple modification of the score allows the same framework to establish tight lower bounds for all three error measures.

669aaae20844c209ea4cbdac.title_original: Optimal Additive Integer Masks for One-Guess Vulnerability under an Absolute-Moment Budget
669aaae20844c209ea4cbdac.excerpt: arXiv:2611.16066v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We study the average one-guess success probability of an adversary who observes the ordinary integer sum of a finite-support secret and an independent integer-valued mask, subject to an absolute-moment budget on the mask. For a uniform secret on an interval the exact optimum and an explicit optimiser are obtained. For a biased bit the masks that achieve no increase over the prior baseline are characterised, and the entire cost--vulnerability frontier is determined. It is the piecewise-linear interpolation of an explicit sequence of points generated by cost-optimally shifted truncated geometric masks. It has infinitely many affine pieces, which accumulate at the critical cost, where the frontier meets the prior baseline with zero slope. The proof rests on a layer-cake decomposition of an arbitrary mask into truncated geometrics, along which both the vulnerability and the cost are exactly additive. The results give exact design guidance for additive integer noise under the average one-guess metric.

ed695ca7f6e34bc7113bc07d.title_original: The challenge of defending against bulletproof dead drops on public blockchains
ed695ca7f6e34bc7113bc07d.excerpt: The evolution of malware command-and-control (C2) infrastructure has shifted away from fragile, centralized servers and hardcoded domains toward resilient, decentralized blockchain networks that eliminate single points of failure. Threat actors are leveraging immutable public ledgers such as Bitcoin transactions, EVM smart contracts via techniques like EtherHiding, TRON wallets, and Solana memo programs to store, mask, and persistently update their operational endpoints. By executing read-only remote procedure call (RPC) queries to retrieve encrypted C2 configurations directly into compromised endpoint memory, adversaries can continuously bypass traditional perimeter defenses and domain seizures. Modern cybersecurity requires a fundamental shift away from static domain blocklists toward monitoring anomalous outbound JSON-RPC traffic, analyzing endpoint memory, and treating blockchain infrastructure as an active threat communication channel. The command-and-control (C2) channel is the operational backbone of any persistent malware campaign. It is also the most fragile component. The moment an actor's C2 infrastructure is identified and reported to the hosting provider, the domain registrar, or law enforcement, the campaign's operational capability collapses. This fundamental asymmetry, where defenders need to identify only a single infrastructure link to disrupt an operation, has driven a multi-decade arms race in resilience techniques, spanning from fast flux DNS evasion to decentralized and peer-to-peer architectures. Traditional C2 infrastructure where malware beacons to a hardcoded domain or IP address is volatile by design. Security researchers or incident responders who identify the C2 address can trigger a response. The hosting provider can null-route the IP addresses and the domain registrars can suspend malicious domains under abuse policies, law enforcement can obtain court orders compelling infrastructure seizure, and threat intelligence vendors push blocklist updates that cut off the malware from its C2 links across several compromised endpoints simultaneously. This single point of failure model renders sophisticated malware families inactive once their C2 is identified and sinkholed. By redirecting malware traffic to researcher-controlled servers, researchers can not only disrupt the botnet but map the full victim community, gather forensic telemetry, and notify affected organizations. The arms race Threat actors have progressively hardened their C2 infrastructure through several evasion techniques to outpace defensive capabilities. Amongst these techniques, some of the popular approaches include the employment of domain generation algorithms (DGA), content delivery network (CDN) domain fronting, peer-to-peer (P2P) architecture, and dead drop resolvers. DGAs replace static, hardcoded server domains with dynamically generated domains. Malware programmed with a shared mathematical seed computes hundreds or thousands of pseudorandom domain names on a scheduled basis, systematically attempting to resolve each one until it establishes contact with an address registered by the threat actor. While this technique prevents defenders from neutralizing an entire operation by simply seizing or blocklisting a single domain, defenders counteracted DGAs by reverse engineering the generation algorithms, predicting future domains for proactive sinkholing, and applying machine learning models to detect algorithmically generated strings within enterprise DNS queries. The CDN domain fronting technique evolved to bypass perimeter inspection mechanisms by exploiting discrepancies between the transport and application layers of encrypted web traffic. By initiating a TLS handshake with a legitimate, reputable domain hosted on a major CDN and specifying a covert, malicious host inside the encrypted HTTP Host header, threat actors route communications through benign enterprise traffic profiles. Enterprise security tools inspecting the outer connection perceive only standard communication with a trusted global platform, effectively masking the true destination behind high reputation infrastructure. However, major cloud providers and network carriers have largely dismantled this evasion vector by standardizing routing policies and enforcing strict matching between TLS Server Name indication values and internal request headers. P2P architectures eliminate the single point of failure in a centralized server altogether by structuring infected hosts into a decentralized, self-healing mesh network. Instead of querying a primary server for instructions, compromised nodes propagate operational commands, binary updates, and collected data directly between adjacent peers using custom overlay routing protocols. This distributed topology ensures that severing dozens or even hundreds of individual endpoints leave the broader network intact and functional. Nevertheless, peer-to-peer networks suffer from inherent architectural exposure, because defenders and security researchers can enumerate the entire topology by acting as benign nodes, map peer lists, and progressively isolate the infected nodes. Dead drop resolvers establish an indirect channel by abusing established third-party web services as covert repositories for downstream infrastructure coordinates. Rather than communicating with an adversary's operational network directly, deployed malware retrieves encoded or encrypted IP addresses and domain names embedded inside public social media bios, code repository commits, or image metadata. By masking this initial discovery phase behind legitimate user activity on high-traffic consumer platforms, attackers blind simple reputation-based network defenses. Defenders eventually contain dead drop tactics by working directly with service providers to enforce aggressive account suspension, remove flagged content, and monitor automated outbound API requests from internal enterprise endpoints. The actor’s arsenal has several payloads including the Go-based Overlord remote access trojan (RAT), a Python-based infostealer internally labelled “Good Game,” and a multi-cryptocurrency clipboard hijacker. The threat actor is likely operating a campaign targeting cryptocurrency holders, gaming platform account owners, and VoIP software users based on the lure file names of the initial vectors and the payloads. The Overlord RAT implements a command-and-control (C2) resilience technique in which encrypted server URLs are embedded in Solana blockchain transaction memos. Victimology The threat actor is potentially targeting victims in Europe, according to the payload’s keyword-based file harvesting capability, which specifically targeted documents that had file names in English, French, Spanish, and Portuguese. Based on the lure themes and payload file names, the potential victim pool spans across multiple verticals. A lure financial statement decoy PDF — launched when the Good Game stealer is executed — indicates targeting finance and accounting staff. The Viber trojanized installer lure targets messaging platform users, while additional payload variants of files named microsip indicate targeting VoIP softphone operators, consistent with call-center or business telephone environments. Cryptocurrency and gaming users are also targeted by both the clipboard hijacker and the infostealer. The Overlord RAT variant observed in this campaign implements a blockchain C2 resilience technique with Solana blockchain transactions. This technique was first reported in March 2026 , employed by the Lazarus APT group. Although the implementation methodology differs (earlier, it was through Node.js), the technique of leveraging Solana transaction memo stayed consistent. Talos is aware that Overlord RAT and Solana blockchain hosting technique is also leveraged by other threat actors in their campaigns, as reported by external security researchers in October 2026 . Threat actor infrastructure Talos observed that the actor hosted the malicious files on a server with IP address “41[.]216[.]188[.]11”, running a Flask-based file delivery service on port 8000 with resumable byte-range download support, and serving the payload staging directory. Due to the actor’s operational security failure, the server’s root folder was exposed to the internet, and Talos’ analysis of the exposed folder showed us actor’s tool sets, and the port numbers configured on the C2 server for different services. The actor used the discord webhook, which receives an immediate notification that contains a victim’s fingerprint and a single click download link. The stolen data archive is uploaded to “gofile[.]io” and is later accessed by the actor through the download link. 27e4a4a5ed9fdfdbc435b199.title_original: CVE-2026-123007: Critical NGINX HTTP/2 Integer Underflow Leads to RCE (FIXED)
27e4a4a5ed9fdfdbc435b199.excerpt: Overview Today, both Rapid7 and F5 are disclosing CVE-2026-123007 , a critical integer underflow vulnerability affecting nginx HTTP/2, which can allow for unauthenticated remote code execution (RCE) against affected servers under certain conditions. CVE ID Description CWE CVSSv4 CVE-2026-123007 HTTP/2 flow-control memory corruption permitting worker-context RCE CWE-191 (Integer Underflow) 9.2 (Critical) nginx can miscalculate how much response data an HTTP/2 client has allowed it to send. A remote, unauthenticated client can exploit this error by cancelling queued response data, then make nginx use an invalid length when copying a later response. The resulting memory corruption can disclose data, interrupt service, and execute code with the nginx worker process's permissions. Impact Rapid7 has developed a proof-of-concept to demonstrate leveraging CVE-2026-123007 for unauthenticated RCE against a vulnerable linux/amd64 Docker image running nginx version 1.31.8 , as shown below in Figure 1. The target nginx server’s configuration had http2 on and TLS enabled. Note that for brevity, video playback is at 8x speed. Figure 1: Video demonstrating unauthenticated RCE against NGINX 1.31.8 via CVE-2026-123007 Leveraging CVE-2026-123007 for RCE requires a significant amount of network traffic to be transmitted, approximately 128 GB of HTTP/2 data. Both available network bandwidth and connection timeouts will place practical limitations on Internet exploitation. In the above example shown in Figure 1, exploitation takes two and a half minutes. The approximate timings to transmit the required network data over a 10 Gbit/s network is two minutes, while on a 1 Gbit/s network it is seventeen minutes. Due to nginx’s default one hour connection lifetime, a network slower than approximately 300 Mbit/s will take over the one hour connection limit threshold and will not be able to succeed. Additionally, should an HTTP/2 connection be proxied, the precise attacker-controlled HTTP/2 frames being transmitted will likely not be retransmitted in a way that satisfies exploiting the vulnerability. Finally, the exploitation strategy developed depends on a specific x86-64 glibc EVEX/YMM memcpy implementation selected at runtime, based on the avx512f and avx512vl CPU features. Alternative RCE exploitation strategies may be viable, but none are currently known. Credit This vulnerability was discovered by Stephen Fewer, Senior Principal Security Researcher at Rapid7 , and is being disclosed in accordance with Rapid7's vulnerability disclosure policy . Technical analysis The version of nginx tested was a linux/amd64 Docker image for nginx version 1.31.8 ( nginx@sha256:5ab5b0b01097420873a3f3330f44248e34a3c2a3e8d5ee30658aeae8cb7435da ), and ran with an exposed HTTPS service and http2 enabled. How a client controls HTTP/2 response data HTTP/2 carries messages called frames over a connection. Each request and response belongs to a numbered stream, so one connection can carry several exchanges at once. Response-body bytes are carried in DATA frames. For this vulnerability, nginx is the sender and the remote client is the receiver. The client grants nginx permission, or flow-control credit, to send a certain number of DATA bytes. nginx tracks the remaining credit in two counters: one for each stream and one shared by the connection. Sending DATA must be permitted by both counters. These HTTP/2 counters are separate from TCP's receive window. The client grants more credit by sending a WINDOW_UPDATE frame containing a positive increment. A stream identifier of zero increases the connection’s send credit. A nonzero stream identifier increases the send credit for the stream with that specific nonzero identifier. HTTP/2 limits the increment and the resulting window to 2^31-1 bytes, or 2,147,483,647 (0x7FFFFFFF). This report calls that maximum MAX . The client can also send a SETTINGS frame containing a SETTINGS_INITIAL_WINDOW_SIZE parameter. This changes the starting credit for new streams. nginx must also adjust each active stream's remaining credit by the difference between the old and new setting values. It does not change the connection's credit. A reduction can therefore leave an active stream with negative credit until the client grants more. The connection window has no equivalent reduction: it must remain between zero and MAX . RFC 9113, section 6.9 defines these limits and the required errors. nginx stores the connection counter in h2c->send_window , where h2c is the HTTP/2 connection record. Its size_t type is an unsigned integer: on the verified 64-bit build it can hold values from zero to 2^64-1 . The size_t type can therefore hold values above HTTP/2's maximum connection window of 2^31-1 bytes ( MAX ). nginx must enforce that protocol limit in its own logic. // src/http/v2/ngx_http_v2.h #define NGX_HTTP_V2_MAX_WINDOW ((1U << 31) - 1) // <--- [1] struct ngx_http_v2_connection_s { // ... size_t send_window; // <--- [2] // ... }; struct ngx_http_v2_stream_s { // ... ssize_t send_window; // ... }; The rule that the connection counter at [2] must never exceed MAX at [1] is the connection-window invariant. The separate stream counter, stream->send_window , is explicitly declared as ssize_t , a signed 64-bit integer on the verified build. That allows SETTINGS_INITIAL_WINDOW_SIZE to make a stream's credit temporarily negative. The connection counter remains unsigned. The later unsafe conversion occurs when the output filter treats excessive connection credit as a signed 64-bit off_t response length. Leveraging vulnerability has four main stages: By slowing its reading of server output, the client keeps selected DATA frames queued and unstarted. It raises the connection's credit to MAX and the selected streams' credit to just below MAX . 7bfd7a1d711f081c03eca426.title_original: Goodhart in the Planner: Sampling-Based Control Exploits Rewards Learned from Human Preferences
7bfd7a1d711f081c03eca426.excerpt: arXiv:2611.09670v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Robots increasingly plan by searching against a reward model learned from human preferences. We measure what this search does to the true objective. On HalfCheetah and Hopper with crowd-sourced labels, and on Meta-World drawer-open and plate-slide with synthetic and blind human labels, harder MPPI search cuts true return by up to 76% while held-out label accuracy stays at 0.75-0.97; with human labels the drawer opens in 0 of 20 runs, against 10 of 10 for the cloned policy the planner starts from. The effect persists with a learned dynamics model and an image scorer. We prove that $\chi^2$-regularized MPPI at a temperature set by the scorer's error spread on the proposals is worst-case optimal, and that no gain can be certified once that spread exceeds the scorer's own. Calibrated from 100 ranked proposal pairs, this rule is the safest fix we test, keeping 86-94% of the cloned policy's return on drawer-open and plate-slide.

9e9f15d38d433e570d1e8a30.title_original: OverServe: Resource Amplification Attacks on SaaS Agents via Tool--Prompt Co-Design
9e9f15d38d433e570d1e8a30.excerpt: arXiv:2611.14808v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Advances in large language models (LLMs) are enabling software-as-a-service (SaaS) providers to automate longer business workflows with agents. In subscription-based SaaS deployments, model and tool calls consume provider resources without additional customer payments. Because the agent autonomously decides when to stop, a malicious tenant can send a prompt to the agent, exploiting its completion decisions to extend execution and waste provider resources. In this paper, we present OverServe, a multi-agent framework for constructing such attacks against SaaS agents. OverServe co-designs Model Context Protocol (MCP) status tools and completion-confirmation prompts for the attacker. Each tool call returns accurate status and terminates normally, yet the agent may repeatedly check an unfinished condition to satisfy the prompt. This consumes the SaaS provider's resources even after the original business task is completed. OverServe constructs service-specific tool--prompt pairs and uses separate tool and prompt reviews to guide candidate pair selection. Tested tool specifications trigger no alerts in the evaluated MCP scanners. We evaluate Qwen, Nemotron, DeepSeek, and Sonnet on selected tasks from nine benchmarks. All OverServe runs pass the original task checks. OverServe can reach a maximal amplification of API requests by $93.88\times$ while preserving the original task goal and collateral checks.
