8056e1e8b9532b688d3f2899.title_original: 엔진엑스(NGINX), 원격 코드 실행 가능한 ‘NGINX2Root’ 취약점(CVE-2026-123007 외 5건) 긴급 업데이트 권고
8056e1e8b9532b688d3f2899.excerpt: 생성형 AI 제작 이미지 F5가 웹 서버 소프트웨어 NGINX(엔진엑스)에서 발견된 원격 코드 실행 취약점 5건(CVE-2026-123007 등, 일명 NGINX2Root)에 대한 보안 업데이트를 배포했습니다. 이번 취약점은 NGINX의 HTTP/2·HTTP/3 처리 모듈, 이름 확인(resolver) 기능, 메일 프록시 모듈에서 발생하는 메모리 손상 결함으로, 인증 없이 원격에서 조작된 요청을 보내 NGINX 작업 프로세스(worker)를 중단시키거나, 메모리 주소 무작위화(ASLR)가 꺼져 있거나 우회되는 환경에서는 임의 코드를 실행할 수 있습니다. F5는 5건 모두 CVSS 4.0 기준 9.2점(Critical), CVSS 3.1 기준 8.1점(High)으로 평가했으며, 한국인터넷진흥원(KISA)도 보안 업데이트 권고를 발표했습니다. 취약점을 발견한 보안업체 Xint는 대표 취약점(CVE-2026-123007)으로 클라우드 서버를 원격 공격해 명령 실행에 성공했고, 별도의 리눅스 커널 취약점과 연계해 루트 권한까지 획득했다고 밝혔습니다. NGINX는 웹 서버, 리버스 프록시, 로드밸런서, 쿠버네티스 인그레스 등 외부 요청이 가장 먼저 도달하는 위치에서 널리 쓰이는 만큼, 운영자분들은 아래 내용을 참고해 신속하게 보안 업데이트를 적용하시기 바랍니다. 취약점 개요 CVE CVE-2026-123007, CVE-2026-123634, CVE-2026-123633, CVE-2026-121810, CVE-2026-113425 (일명 NGINX2Root) 영향 컴포넌트 NGINX Plus, NGINX Open Source 및 이를 포함한 F5 NGINX 제품 ngx_http_v2_module , ngx_http_v3_module , NGINX resolver, ngx_mail_proxy_module 취약점 유형 정수 언더플로로 인한 힙 버퍼 오버플로(1건), 해제된 메모리 사용(Use After Free, 4건) 작업 프로세스 중단(서비스 거부), 메모리 손상, 원격 코드 실행 가능 공격 조건 네트워크, 인증 불필요, 사용자 개입 불필요, 공격 복잡도 높음 취약점별로 HTTP/2·HTTP/3 사용, 메일 프록시 사용 등 특정 설정에서만 해당 심각도 Critical (CVSS v4.0 9.2) / High (CVSS v3.1 8.1) - F5 평가 (5건 동일) CVSS:4.0/AV:N/AC:H/AT:N/PR:N/UI:N/VC:H/VI:H/VA:H/SC:N/SI:N/SA:N 영향 대상 NGINX Open Source 1.30.6 이하, 1.31.0 ~ 1.31.8 NGINX Plus 37.0.0 ~ 37.2.0.1 및 R34 ~ R36 공개일 2026. 11. 18. (미국 시간, F5 보안 권고 발표) 실제 악용 실제 공격에 악용된 사례는 보고되지 않음 (2026. 11. 19. 기준, CISA KEV 미등재) 조치 NGINX Open Source 1.30.7 / 1.31.9, NGINX Plus 37.0.8.1 / 37.3.0.1 이상으로 업데이트 후 NGINX 재시작 CVE-2026-123634, CVE-2026-113425는 F5가 안내한 설정 변경으로 임시 완화 가능 취약점 상세정보 ■ 취약점 발생 원인 이번 취약점 5건은 서로 다른 모듈에서 발생하지만, 모두 NGINX가 요청을 처리하는 작업 프로세스(worker)의 메모리를 손상시킨다는 공통점이 있습니다. F5는 5건 모두 공격자가 작업 프로세스를 중단시킬 수 있고, ASLR이 비활성화되어 있거나 공격자가 ASLR을 우회할 수 있는 경우 코드 실행까지 가능하다고 밝혔습니다. CVE 취약 모듈 원인 (F5 권고문 기준) CVE-2026-123007 ngx_http_v2_module HTTP/2 처리 중 흐름 제어 윈도(flow control window)가 허용 범위를 넘어서면서 정수 언더플로(CWE-191)가 발생해 힙 버퍼 오버플로로 이어짐 CVE-2026-123634 NGINX resolver 프록시 대상 서버 이름에 변수를 쓰고, SSI 또는 mirror 지시어가 같은 서버 이름으로 하위 요청을 보낼 때 조작된 HTTP 요청으로 해제된 메모리를 사용(CWE-416) CVE-2026-123633 ngx_http_v2_module 클라이언트 연결에 HTTP/2를 쓰고 요청을 백엔드로 프록시하는 환경에서, 작업 프로세스의 연결 수(worker_connections)가 부족할 때 조작된 요청으로 해제된 메모리를 사용(CWE-416) CVE-2026-121810 ngx_http_v3_module HTTP/3 사용 환경에서 원격의 인증되지 않은 공격자가 해제된 메모리 사용(CWE-416)을 유발. 공격자가 통제할 수 없는 조건도 필요 CVE-2026-113425 ngx_mail_proxy_module 메일 프록시로 구성된 환경에서 조작된 메일 세션으로 해제된 메모리를 사용(CWE-416) [표 1] NGINX2Root 취약점별 발생 원인 이 중 가장 영향 범위가 넓은 취약점은 CVE-2026-123007입니다. HTTP/2는 클라이언트와 서버가 서로 보낼 수 있는 데이터 양(흐름 제어 윈도)을 주고받으며 통신하는데, NGINX가 이 값을 처리하는 과정에서 계산이 어긋나 메모리 범위를 벗어난 쓰기가 발생합니다. Xint의 분석에 따르면 클라이언트가 보내는 WINDOW_UPDATE 프레임과 스트림 취소(RST_STREAM)를 조작하면 서버의 전송 윈도가 최댓값을 넘어서게 되고, 결국 잘못된 메모리 복사 길이가 만들어져 힙 메모리 범위를 벗어난 읽기·쓰기가 발생합니다. 이 코드는 NGINX가 HTTP/2를 처음 도입한 1.9.5(2015년)부터 10년 넘게 존재해 왔습니다. 단계 동작 ① 조작된 요청 전송 공격자가 HTTP/2가 활성화된 NGINX에 조작된 HTTP/2 제어 프레임(WINDOW_UPDATE, RST_STREAM 등)을 전송 ② 흐름 제어 값 오계산 흐름 제어 윈도 값이 허용 범위를 넘어서면서 정수 언더플로 발생 ③ 힙 버퍼 오버플로 잘못된 값으로 메모리를 처리하면서 힙 메모리 범위를 벗어난 쓰기 발생 ④ 결과 작업 프로세스 비정상 종료(서비스 거부) → ASLR 비활성화·우회 시 원격 코드 실행 [표 2] CVE-2026-123007 발생 흐름 ■ 영향 및 공격 시나리오 F5에 따르면 이번 취약점은 실제 트래픽을 처리하는 데이터 영역(data plane)의 문제이며, 관리 영역(control plane)은 노출되지 않습니다. 공격자는 인증 없이 네트워크로 조작된 요청을 보내는 것만으로 작업 프로세스를 반복적으로 중단시켜 서비스 장애를 일으킬 수 있고, ASLR이 꺼져 있거나 우회 가능한 환경에서는 NGINX 작업 프로세스 권한으로 임의 코드를 실행할 수 있습니다. 다만 F5는 공격 복잡도를 '높음'으로 평가했으며, 각 취약점은 특정 기능을 사용하는 설정에서만 해당합니다. NGINX는 외부 요청이 가장 먼저 도달하는 위치에 있기 때문에, 공격에 성공하면 복호화된 요청·응답(비밀번호, 세션 토큰 등)에 접근하거나 NGINX를 신뢰하는 내부 백엔드 시스템을 공격하는 발판으로 악용될 수 있습니다. 취약점을 발견한 Xint는 AWS 환경에서 공인 IP로 노출된 서버를 대상으로 CVE-2026-123007을 이용해 NGINX 작업 프로세스 권한으로 명령을 실행하는 과정을 시연했습니다. 또한 2018년 리눅스 커널 4.15부터 존재해 온 SCTP 기능의 메모리 손상 취약점과 연계해 루트 권한을 획득했으며, Docker 컨테이너에서 실행 중인 NGINX에서도 컨테이너를 벗어나 호스트의 루트 권한을 얻었다고 밝혔습니다. Xint는 NGINX 취약점 5건과 이 커널 취약점 1건을 묶어 NGINX2Root라고 이름 붙였으며, 커널 취약점은 아직 패치가 공개되지 않았습니다. Xint가 Shodan으로 조사한 결과, 버전 정보를 확인할 수 있는 NGINX 서버 약 1,194만 대 가운데 98.9%가 CVE-2026-123007의 영향 버전 범위(1.9.5 ~ 1.31.8)에 해당했습니다. 다만 이는 노출된 버전 문자열 기준이며, 실제 취약 여부는 HTTP/2 사용 여부와 배포판 백포트 패치 적용 여부에 따라 달라집니다. 영향 받는 버전 및 패치 버전 이번 취약점은 NGINX 버전과 함께, 각 취약점에 해당하는 기능을 사용하는 설정일 때만 영향을 받습니다. ■ 영향 조건 CVE 영향 설정 NGINX Open Source 영향 버전 CVE-2026-123007 HTTP/2 사용 1.9.5 ~ 1.30.6, 1.31.0 ~ 1.31.8 CVE-2026-123634 프록시 대상 서버 이름에 변수 사용 + SSI 또는 mirror 지시어 사용 0.6.18 ~ 1.30.6, 1.31.0 ~ 1.31.8 CVE-2026-123633 클라이언트 연결에 HTTP/2 사용 + 백엔드로 프록시 1.19.7 ~ 1.30.6, 1.31.0 ~ 1.31.8 CVE-2026-121810 HTTP/3 사용 1.25.0 ~ 1.30.6, 1.31.0 ~ 1.31.8 CVE-2026-113425 메일 프록시 서버로 사용 0.5.33 ~ 1.30.6, 1.31.0 ~ 1.31.8 [표 3] NGINX2Root 취약점별 영향 조건 ■ NGINX Open Source / NGINX Plus 제품 영향 받는 버전 패치 버전 NGINX Open Source (mainline) 1.31.0 ~ 1.31.8 1.31.9 NGINX Open Source (stable) 1.30.6 이하 1.30.7 NGINX Plus 37.1 이상 37.1.0 ~ 37.2.0.1 37.3.0.1 NGINX Plus 37.0 37.0.0 ~ 37.0.7.1 37.0.8.1 NGINX Plus R 시리즈 R34 ~ R36 패치 없음 (37.x 패치 버전으로 업그레이드) [표 4] NGINX Open Source / NGINX Plus 영향 받는 버전 및 패치 버전 NGINX Open Source는 1.30.7과 1.31.9에서 5건이 모두 수정되었으며, 1.29.x 이하의 이전 버전은 별도 패치가 없으므로 패치 버전으로 업그레이드해야 합니다. NGINX Plus는 CVE-2026-123633(37.2.0.1, 37.0.7.1부터 수정)과 CVE-2026-113425(37.3.0, 37.0.8부터 수정)의 패치 버전이 다른 취약점보다 앞서므로, 37.3.0.1 또는 37.0.8.1 이상을 적용하면 5건이 모두 해결됩니다. F5는 기술 지원이 종료된 버전은 평가하지 않았습니다. ■ NGINX 기반 F5 제품 제품 영향 받는 버전 패치 버전 NGINX Instance Manager 2.19.0 ~ 2.24.1 2.25.0 F5 WAF for NGINX 5.9.0 ~ 5.16.1 5.16.2, 5.14.4 F5 DoS for NGINX 4.8.0 ~ 4.12.0 4.13.0 NGINX Gateway Fabric 2.0.0 ~ 2.8.1 1.5.0 ~ 1.6.2 2.9.0 패치 없음 NGINX Ingress Controller 2026-lts-r1 ~ 2026-lts-r10 5.0.0 ~ 5.7.1 4.0.0 ~ 4.0.1, 3.7.1 ~ 3.7.2 2026-lts-r11 5.8.0 패치 없음 NGINX App Protect WAF 5.4.0 ~ 5.8.0, 4.12.0 ~ 4.16.0 패치 없음 NGINX App Protect DoS 4.5.0 ~ 4.7.0 패치 없음 [표 5] NGINX 기반 F5 제품 영향 받는 버전 및 패치 버전 패치가 없는 버전은 F5가 패치 버전이 있는 버전으로 업그레이드하도록 권고하고 있습니다. BIG-IP, BIG-IQ, F5OS 등 그 밖의 F5 제품은 영향을 받지 않으며, F5 Distributed Cloud와 NGINX One Console은 일부 취약점에 대해 F5가 영향 여부를 확인 중입니다. 또한 리눅스 배포판 패키지와 NGINX를 내장한 다른 제품은 배포처마다 패치 일정과 버전 표기가 다르므로 각 배포처의 보안 공지를 확인해야 합니다. 조치 방법 ■ 점검 우선순위 인터넷에 노출되어 HTTP/2·HTTP/3로 요청을 받는 NGINX 서버부터 우선 점검합니다. 구분 대상 노출 조건 우선순위 외부 노출 인터넷에 노출된 NGINX 웹

7c62bcc10ac6af3e22878207.title_original: PSA: Critical NGINX HTTP/2 Vulnerabilities: What WordPress Site Owners Should Know
7c62bcc10ac6af3e22878207.excerpt: NGINX has released fixes for two critical HTTP/2 vulnerabilities, CVE-2026-123007 and CVE-2026-123633 . Both can lead to remote code execution on affected servers. If your WordPress site uses NGINX, keep an eye out for guidance from your hosting provider about whether its servers are affected and patched. NGINX lists versions 1.9.5–1.30.6 and 1.31.0–1.31.8 as affected by CVE-2026-123007; CVE-2026-123633 starts at 1.19.7 . Fixed open-source versions 1.30.7 (stable) and 1.31.9 (mainline) were released November 18, 2026. Both flaws require NGINX to accept client HTTP/2. CVE-2026-123633 also requires forwarding requests to a backend while a worker runs low on connections. HTTP/2 is off unless a server’s configuration enables it. NGINX’s source build omits the HTTP/2 module by default , but NGINX’s own prebuilt packages include it , and hosting configurations vary. Why This Is Important for WordPress Sites NGINX can serve a WordPress site or sit in front of its application server. It handles HTTP/2 before requests reach PHP or WordPress. Successful exploitation could run code with the NGINX worker’s privileges, putting sites and data on that server at risk. Updating WordPress, plugins, themes, or Wordfence will not patch NGINX. The Wordfence firewall runs at the PHP application layer . Your host or server administrator must install the server fix; a Wordfence scan cannot confirm its patch status. What We Know F5 rates CVE-2026-123007 Critical at 9.2 under CVSS v4.0, and its second advisory gives CVE-2026-123633 the same rating. Wiz reports lab code execution for both flaws; Metnir reports it for CVE-2026-123633. Rapid7 published an RCE proof of concept for CVE-2026-123007, tailored to a freshly started local Docker target. Its demonstrated method needs substantial traffic, but that does not rule out other methods. Xint , which F5 credits for CVE-2026-123007, reports code execution over public HTTPS on AWS, GCP, and Azure under concurrent normal traffic. It also reports chaining the NGINX flaw with a separate Linux kernel bug to gain root in its tests. CERT-EU reported no known exploitation in the wild on November 18. How to Check Whether Your Server Is Exposed WordPress Site Health cannot confirm whether your host’s NGINX package is patched or whether the server accepts HTTP/2. If you use managed or shared hosting, watch your provider’s security announcements and status updates for guidance on these CVEs. If no update is available yet, continue monitoring its official channels. If you manage the server, check its NGINX package and active HTTP/2 configuration, including reverse proxies and containers. Follow your vendor’s advisory: backported fixes may retain older NGINX version numbers. A site’s public HTTP/2 connection may terminate at a CDN rather than the NGINX origin; check the origin and any direct route to it. What to Do Now Managed or shared hosting: Watch for your host’s security announcements and follow any guidance it provides about these CVEs. Self-managed NGINX: Install 1.30.7, 1.31.9, or your vendor’s fixed package, then restart NGINX to load the new binary. Recreate containers from patched images. For NGINX Plus, check F5’s fixed releases for CVE-2026-123007 and CVE-2026-123633 . If you manage NGINX and cannot update yet: Temporarily disable HTTP/2 on affected NGINX listeners. Remove http2 from relevant listen directives; on NGINX 1.25.1 or later, also set http2 off; . Test and reload the configuration, then verify HTTP/2 is no longer accepted. This does not address other vulnerabilities fixed in the same NGINX release. Timeline August 29, 2026: Metnir says it found CVE-2026-123633 . September 12, 2026: Metnir reported CVE-2026-123633 to F5. October 11, 2026: Xint says it discovered CVE-2026-123007 . October 16, 2026: Xint reported its findings to F5 through HackerOne. November 18, 2026: NGINX released versions 1.30.7 and 1.31.9 with fixes for both HTTP/2 flaws. Conclusion If your WordPress site uses NGINX, watch for your hosting provider’s guidance on these CVEs. Server administrators should install a fixed NGINX or vendor package and restart NGINX. Disabling HTTP/2 temporarily blocks these two attack paths, but does not address other vulnerabilities fixed in the same release. The post PSA: Critical NGINX HTTP/2 Vulnerabilities: What WordPress Site Owners Should Know appeared first on Wordfence .

907bdda16bd7be03d1a74a36.title_original: Human-AI Mutualism Is Unstable under Capability Asymmetry
907bdda16bd7be03d1a74a36.excerpt: arXiv:2611.23322v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: One hope for a good human future alongside advanced AI rests on enduring mutualism: humans and AI will need each other, so the relationship will stay good for both. We argue that this hope fails as AI capability grows. Bargaining guarantees each side only what it would get if bargaining failed. For humans, this can be less than they had before AI. In a simple game-theoretic model, humans stay as well off as before AI without alignment only while they have leverage over the AI: either the AI depends on what they supply, or they can impose costs on the AI that are large relative to what the AI can produce. Once humans have neither kind of leverage, they stay as well off as before AI only if the AI is aligned with them. If the AI's goals are insatiable, the alignment required approaches perfect alignment as AI capability grows. Thus, mutualism is not a substitute for alignment. And when AI variants that keep more resources spread faster, alignment lasts only while misaligned variants are reliably sanctioned. In these two senses, human-AI mutualism is unstable.

6dbf900545ddda3f5f8c82ad.title_original: Training Language Models for Introspective Oversight
6dbf900545ddda3f5f8c82ad.excerpt: arXiv:2611.23365v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Language models increasingly exhibit behaviors that are difficult to detect in transcripts, such as reward hacking, deception, and sycophancy. Asking the assistant follow-up questions about its actions is unreliable, since models are generally not trained to report their own misbehavior. As a result, approaches to oversight typically involve querying external models. These face limitations: external transcript monitoring operates only on visible model outputs, and activation decoders lack full context and are prone to confabulation. We introduce introspective oversight, which trains a new role in the model to answer arbitrary questions about the assistant, rewarding answers that are verified against the assistant's actual behavior. We implement this by adding a separate, third-person observer role that answers these queries, which we can train solely for accuracy and separately from the assistant. On five held-out oversight evaluations, an observer trained on Qwen3.6-27B obtains a mean AUROC of 0.907, outperforming honesty training (0.864), transcript monitoring (0.828), and activation oracles (0.796). We further find that training an observer makes the assistant itself easier to monitor, with every baseline method improving on average when applied to the fine-tuned assistant. These results suggest that training models to answer verifiable questions about themselves is a tractable approach to overseeing unintended behavior.

dfa9794d68dbb778be2c20be.title_original: Where the Tokens Go: Heat, Entropy and Error in Agentic Coding
dfa9794d68dbb778be2c20be.excerpt: arXiv:2611.23375v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Coding agents are billed by the token, yet software engineering says nothing about what a token actually buys. Here we introduce a theory of software thermodynamics. The theory draws analogues from classical and stochastic thermodynamics, extends them, and applies them to modern agentic coding. We count the tokens an agent generates as its cost and divide that cost into work and heat. The test suite acts as a software Maxwell's daemon that judges every coding change. We test the theory with an analogue of the experiments in which a single molecule is pulled open and let fold again: an agent makes a change to a repository (coding) and then undoes it (uncoding), many times over, and we count the tokens of every model call. The cycle returns the requested edits to where they began, with each direction started from a stored reference tree, and the spread of its cost over repeated cycles defines a software temperature, which rose with the sampling temperature of the model. About 80 per cent of the tokens of a successful run are generated in model calls that leave the requested change where it was, and we call these tokens heat. The free energy of a change, which we estimate by analogy with the equality of Jarzynski, is 14 to 22 per cent of the mean cost of a successful coding run. Coding costs 1.1 to 1.5 times as much as uncoding. The daemon is imperfect: the verdict of a test suite varies with its environment, and a suite that accepts a broken change has a cost in tokens. The practical implication of the proposed theory could be new tools for analysing and optimising coding agents through the lens of thermodynamics.

c4ff0d58a83abb8b18230c30.title_original: HardwareDx: A Foundational Graph Model System for Datacenter Machine Repairs
c4ff0d58a83abb8b18230c30.excerpt: arXiv:2611.23398v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The rapid scale-up of AI infrastructure has made datacenter reliability a cornerstone of the cloud business economy. Since hardware failures in hyper-scale AI clusters can stall multi-million dollar training workloads, the downtime of individual machines can cause outsized economic losses. Minimizing machine downtime, therefore, is more important than ever. To address this, we present Hardware Diagnoser (HardwareDx), an AI-driven hardware diagnosis system that applies a graph foundation model approach to automated datacenter maintenance. It allows a single model to diagnose many platforms and accelerate onboarding of new hardware products. Deployed at production scale at Google, HardwareDx yields substantial efficiency gains across diverse compute architectures. Real-world evaluations demonstrate that it reduces production downtime by 18.3% on GPU platforms and 16.1% on TPUs. Furthermore, it significantly accelerates hardware deployment, cutting quality assurance (QA) time by 28.3% for GPUs and 25.1% for TPUs. These results establish HardwareDx as a field-tested solution for maximizing the reliability and cost efficiency of next generation AI fleets.

31251aaec544bfe8a37763dc.title_original: RFBench: A Simulator-Grounded Multimodal Benchmark for Passive RF Layout Design and Understanding
31251aaec544bfe8a37763dc.excerpt: arXiv:2611.23410v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: While multimodal language models can interpret diagrams and generate structured outputs, their capacity to connect passive radio-frequency (RF) design intent, layout geometry, and electromagnetic behavior remains largely untested. To address this gap, we introduce RFBench, a simulator-grounded dataset and benchmark for passive RF layout design and understanding. The dataset contains 10,000 two-port planar layouts simulated using ADS Momentum, with each layout represented by editable geometric primitives, a raster image, a 16x16 occupancy grid, complex S-parameters at 201 frequency points, a structural category, and an RF response label. Building on these aligned representations, we define seven tasks spanning specification-conditioned layout generation, representation translation, response prediction, simulator-based validation, design diagnosis and improvement, structural understanding, and response classification. Extensive baselines across seven multimodal language models reveal systematic weaknesses in generating structurally valid layouts and predicting electromagnetically faithful responses. We show that RF-specific fine-tuning increases T1a structural validity from 0.0% to 83.2% and the T3 primitive-input within-2-dB rate from 17.7% to 62.8%, demonstrating the value of domain adaptation while leaving considerable room for further progress. RFBench establishes a common testbed for evaluating multimodal RF capabilities and guiding the development of models that connect design intent and layout representations with physical behavior.

82e645b523188530233b02c7.title_original: Why Sub-4-Bit Vision CNNs Collapse and Where Mixed-Precision Recovery Stops
82e645b523188530233b02c7.excerpt: arXiv:2611.23445v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Deep vision models operating in resource-constrained environments depend heavily on low-bit quantization, yet compressing weights below 4 bits frequently induces catastrophic accuracy collapse. While mixed-precision recovery strategies aim to rescue accuracy by selectively retaining high-precision parameters, the fundamental mechanics of where and why these models collapse remain poorly understood. In this study, we systematically analyze the anatomy of quantization collapse across standard Vision CNNs (including ResNet and EfficientNet backbones) evaluated on the full 50,000-image ImageNet-1k validation set. First, we map the exact progression of degradation, demonstrating that collapse is highly non-linear and concentrated in late-stage pointwise projections and depthwise layers. Second, we introduce a structured, multi-step recovery waterfall that evaluates selective integer precision (INT4/INT8) and selective floating-point scales. We show that keeping less than 5% of critical layer activations in 8-bit precision recovers up to 92% of the accuracy lost during aggressive sub-4-bit compression. Finally, we bridge the hardware reality gap by evaluating deployment performance on standard ARM and x86 CPU architectures. We show that while low-bit quantization reduces memory storage requirements, standard runtime software bit-unpacking introduces a 1.48x to 21.5x execution slowdown depending on batch size, highlighting a critical trade-off between model footprint and actual edge throughput. Our findings provide a practical blueprint for navigating the limits of sub-4-bit deployment without sacrificing hardware performance.

aafc25b0dac82756d18c1fee.title_original: LusoClin: A Synthetic Clinical Note Dataset for Medical Information Retrieval in European Portuguese
aafc25b0dac82756d18c1fee.excerpt: arXiv:2611.23454v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Access to large-scale clinical text collections is crucial for advancing medical information retrieval research, including clinical note search, patient cohort identification, and domain-adapted retrieval models. However, real clinical notes are rarely available due to privacy regulations, which particularly limits progress for low-resource languages such as European Portuguese. We present LusoClin, a publicly released dataset of synthetic clinical notes in European Portuguese, created to support privacy-preserving research on clinical text retrieval. LusoClin was generated by pre-processing real clinical data, fine-tuning the open-source Llama 3.2 (3B) instruction-tuned model using Quantized Low-Rank Adaptation, and applying prompt-based clinical note generation. To facilitate semantic indexing and clinical search, the notes are automatically annotated with clinical entities using a BERT-based model. We evaluate LusoClin in terms of utility, fidelity, diversity, and privacy using automatic metrics and human evaluation. Results indicate that the dataset captures clinically relevant language patterns and can support downstream IR applications such as clinical document retrieval and domain-specific model adaptation, although annotators can often distinguish synthetic from real notes and some medical inconsistencies persist.

12be24d1f9034831991fce36.title_original: VeriMath: Human-in-the-Loop Generation and Verification of Curriculum-Aligned Mathematics Assessment Items
12be24d1f9034831991fce36.excerpt: arXiv:2611.23456v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Automatic generation of mathematics assessment items is a growing area in educational artificial intelligence, yet classroom deployment remains challenging. Generated questions must satisfy multiple constraints: mathematical correctness, curriculum alignment, appropriate cognitive difficulty, and educator reviewability. While prior work has advanced text generation, reliable assessment authoring requires granular control over localized examination formats and expert educational judgment. To address this challenge, we present VeriMath, a generalized, human-in-the-loop framework for generating rigorous, curriculum-constrained mathematics assessment drafts. Using annotated reference items, the framework anchors generation to the requested examination section and cognitive reasoning level, then applies sequential automated verification and guided repair before submitting drafts for expert review. We evaluate VeriMath through a national curriculum case study using 4,555 mathematics items from the Vietnamese Grade 12 curriculum and 50 distinct generation requirements covering multiple-choice, true/false, and short-answer formats. Across two model backbones, the framework produces verifier-accepted drafts for 94% (47/50) of requirements per run. Blind expert evaluations confirm high mathematical accuracy and curriculum alignment, with strict teacher-readiness assessments accepting up to 56.8% of generated items. Analysis of rejected drafts reveals persistent domain-agnostic challenges involving formatting, statement validity, and solution-step completeness. These findings demonstrate that VeriMath can bridge generative AI and dependable educational applications by producing highly reviewable assessment drafts within tightly constrained national curriculum frameworks.

bb9634129567881e68e008a0.title_original: GUARD: Stabilizing Recursive Self-Improvement with Regret Guidance
bb9634129567881e68e008a0.excerpt: arXiv:2611.23476v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Autonomous AI agents pair a frozen base model with an editable harness of prompts, skills, tool rules, and memory. Recursive self-improvement (RSI) adapts this harness from experience without weight updates, yet self-editing without external graders often backfires: reflection and scalar scores conflate what an edit newly broke with what remains unsolved, causing local regressions, skill forgetting, and memory bloat. We introduce GUARD (Grader-free Unsupervised Environment Design [UED] with Adaptive Rule Distillation), a closed-loop framework for reference-free continual harness evolution. Our key insight is to decompose each task into pre-execution self-checks and guide harness updates via directional regret. Each round grades trajectories against these checks, pinning mastered rules while prioritizing newly broken behaviors, and selects among parallel candidate edits by critic-free group-relative fitness. A Soft-HURT gate then promotes an edit only when gains outweigh regressions, scoping specialized fixes to prevent over-triggering and guaranteeing non-regression on its gated buffer. At test time, one frozen harness runs in a single pass. Across benchmarks on memory, skill evolution, continual task streams, and domain reasoning, GUARD consistently improves performance without catastrophic forgetting or memory pollution while substantially cutting deployment token usage.

dc24a888408d107b7aa1ac99.title_original: Diagnostic Accuracy and Navigation Behavior of Vision-Language Model Agents Reading Emergency CT and MRI Examinations
dc24a888408d107b7aa1ac99.excerpt: arXiv:2611.23480v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Purpose. To evaluate the diagnostic accuracy and image navigation behavior of vision-language model (VLM) agents under varying exploration strategies. Materials and Methods. In this retrospective study, six VLMs read 100 emergency CT and MRI examinations published in a public archive (March 2025-August 2026) under four conditions (free navigation, navigation from a key slice, and all slices or key slices in a single request), twice each (4800 runs). Nine radiologists read 30 of those cases. A large language model judge validated against two radiologists graded the answers. Conditions were compared with generalized estimating equations clustered by case. Results. Pooled accuracy was lowest under free navigation (32.6%; 391/1200), followed by navigation from a key slice (37.9%; 455/1200; P = .003), and highest with all slices (42.2%; 506/1200) or key slices (42.5%; 510/1200) in one request (both P < .001). On the 30 cases read by radiologists, freely navigating models were correct in 30.0% of runs (108/360) versus 77.0% for radiologists (208/270; P < .001). Models formed a first hypothesis after a median of 10.8% of the slices and kept it in 63.1% of runs (755/1196); final answers were correct in 12.4% of runs after a wrong first hypothesis (110/885) versus 90.4% after a right one (281/311; P < .001). Median stated confidence in the final answers was 90%, whereas 38.9% of them were correct (1861/4778). Conclusion. Across all exploration strategies, VLM agents remained far less accurate than radiologists. They adopted an early hypothesis and usually kept it, seldom correcting a wrong one.

adf4ca4812370ad8d11c2385.title_original: SpecLook: Speculating Where to Look for Fast and Reliable Agentic MLLMs
adf4ca4812370ad8d11c2385.excerpt: arXiv:2611.23483v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Agentic multimodal large language models (MLLMs) that think with images interleave reasoning with zoom-in tool calls. However, this sequential loop is slow, and its answers carry no reliability score. Prior speculation of tokens, reasoning steps, or answers keeps the loop, and answer speculation also accepts confident errors. We find that the loop mostly adds one zoom-in step, with which a small model is ahead of the agent on most splits. Our key insight is to speculate the agent's next observation, which, unlike a drafted answer, can be verified, corrected, and used to test the answer. We propose SpecLook, a training-free speculate-and-verify framework with three levels. A small model drafts a glimpse and re-answers from it, and the question ends if the answer is unchanged and confident. Otherwise, the agent's large model verifies and corrects the glimpse without tools, and their answers are fused. Only questions that still lack evidence reach the agent, in one forward pass that SpecLook-Fast skips, so no question runs the loop. The trace scores every answer's reliability without labels. Extensive experiments on V*, HR-Bench, and POPE show that both are more accurate than every baseline on every split. SpecLook reaches 87.2% and 86.2% mean accuracy with 7.7x and 4.7x speedups over the DeepEyes-7B and Thyme-RL agents, and SpecLook-Fast reaches 9.9x and 6.3x.

8d9fe1c8714c16d40a8561ec.title_original: BOS Summary: The First Token Matters
8d9fe1c8714c16d40a8561ec.excerpt: arXiv:2611.23508v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large vision-language models (LVLMs) and language models (LLMs) often exhibit attention sinks, whereby particular positions, such as the beginning-of-sequence (BOS) token, receive a disproportionate share of attention. Under standard causal masking, however, the BOS query attends only to itself, so the representation that later tokens repeatedly access carries no information about the input. We introduce BOS Summary, a training-free inference-time method that repurposes this persistent pathway to carry input context. At a single transformer layer during prefill, BOS Summary relaxes the causal constraint for the BOS query row alone, letting BOS aggregate all visual and textual input tokens into a self-derived context representation while every other token retains standard causal attention. The enriched representation then remains accessible to the model throughout decoding, with no additional parameters, auxiliary modules, or decoding-time overhead. Across multiple VLM and LLM families and eight multimodal and text-only benchmarks, BOS Summary improves over direct and Chain-of-Thought prompting and outperforms recent sink-intervention methods on multi-step reasoning tasks. A mechanistic analysis shows that making BOS input-specific also weakens its sink dominance and redistributes attention toward content-bearing prompt tokens, indicating that changing what a sink carries reshapes how later layers allocate attention.

a5f8d369ab0608249013958f.title_original: GRAFT: Execution-Guided Genetic Recombination for Agent Design
a5f8d369ab0608249013958f.excerpt: arXiv:2611.23509v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Automated agent design searches for executable architectures that improve LLM-based agent performance, with evolutionary methods using language-model crossover to recombine promising mechanisms for task decomposition, model coordination, and verification. This search, however, is typically guided by aggregate fitness alone, which hides the instance-level successes and failures behind each score. We introduce Execution Guided Genetic Recombination for Agent Design (GRAFT), which uses aggregate fitness for selection and survival and parent-specific execution evidence to guide semantic crossover with integrated mutation. Its feedback harness reuses bounded samples of successful and failed runs from fitness evaluation, withholding reference answers and requiring no additional task executions. We evaluate GRAFT across six reasoning and programming settings using open-weight optimizer and executor models. It achieves a mean test accuracy of 82.0%, exceeding the strongest baseline by 9.8% points. Controlled ablations show that adding execution evidence improves test accuracy with initialization, search rules, repair policies, and evaluation budgets held fixed. Our results support the value of parent-specific execution evidence for evolutionary agent design.

e86d729e740a90d8577b0ec0.title_original: BeFit: Shifting Complexity from Weights to Bernstein Activations for Resource-Constrained Sensing
e86d729e740a90d8577b0ec0.excerpt: arXiv:2611.23520v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Time-series sensing increasingly relies on neural networks, yet deployment on resource-constrained microcontrollers remains challenging. Aggressive model compression can reduce accuracy, while restricting weights to multiplication-free representations introduces further losses. We present BeFit, an end-to-end framework that shifts model capacity from weights to learnable Bernstein polynomial activations. BeFit (i) finds compact Bernstein-activated convolutional neural networks (BeCNNs) through hardware-aware neural architecture search and trains them via knowledge distillation; (ii) projects their weights to multiplication-free codes, freezes the codes, and recovers the resulting accuracy loss through the learnable activations; and (iii) generates model-specific kernels that exploit the projected weights for multiplication-free convolutions. On human activity recognition, BeCNNs are 2.75 percentage points (pp) more accurate on average than ReLU CNNs of identical architecture. On a TI CC3220SF (Cortex-M4), weight projection speeds BeCNNs up by 2.2x on average while losing 0.8 pp, compared with 2.4 pp for ReLU CNNs. Against the MLPerf Tiny DS-CNN reference model running on TensorFlow Lite Micro with CMSIS-NN, the unprojected BeCNN achieves 1.0 pp higher accuracy, 2.2x lower latency, and 6.4x lower flash, while the projected model remains within 1.0 pp of the reference accuracy and runs 5.9x faster. In emulation on a RISC-V core without a hardware multiplier, the instruction-count reduction relative to the DS-CNN increases from 5.2x on the Cortex-M4 to 147x. BeFit also extends to transformers and MLPs, and across all tasks the final models stay within 1.56 pp of their float32 teachers on average.

482b1404404181d9e9cf90f6.title_original: FACET - Facet Aware Contrastive Embeddings for Traits- Big Five Estimation from Life Narratives
482b1404404181d9e9cf90f6.excerpt: arXiv:2611.23560v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Personality is only weakly and inconsistently signaled by written language, and existing text-based methods typically combine language-model and psycholinguistic representations at the input or decision level. It remains open whether a more deliberate combination of the two views, and a decomposition of the prediction target, can recover more of the signal. We present a three-phase framework for estimating Big Five personality domain scores from life-narrative interview text. It encodes text and psycholinguistic features separately and combines them by concatenation or by a learned weighting, decomposes each domain into contrastively trained facet embeddings instead of predicting the domain directly, and pools the facet embeddings by attention into a domain-level prediction. We compare end-to-end with staged training and ablate the input modalities, their combination, and the facet-pooling strategy. On 1,332 participants from the St. Louis Personality and Aging Network (SPAN) study, facet embeddings reach AUC up to 0.740, and domain-level R2 reaches 0.328, highest for Openness. End-to-end training gives lower error than staged training in every domain, and attention pooling gives the lowest error in every domain. Combining the two views lowers error relative to text alone for Conscientiousness and Agreeableness, whereas a learned weighting of the views shows no consistent advantage over concatenation. The framework provides facet- level predictions that a domain-only model cannot, and it improves modestly on a regression from the raw features in four of the five domains.

a70ec380ba042bbf494d3da6.title_original: LProp: Propagating Latent Uncertainty through Evidence-Conditioned Belief Revision in LLM Agents
a70ec380ba042bbf494d3da6.excerpt: arXiv:2611.23564v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: When LLM agents pass intermediate judgments downstream without uncertainty, later decisions may treat tentative assumptions as facts. Effective uncertainty propagation must preserve information for correction and update inherited beliefs as new evidence arrives. Yet scalar scores omit information needed for revision, while detailed descriptions and reflection incur additional costs. We introduce Latent Uncertainty, a latent-space estimator that preserves uncertainty-relevant information without lengthy descriptions. Building on this, we propose LProp (Latent Uncertainty Propagation), which revises inherited answer distributions using latent representations and new evidence without additional trajectory sampling. We evaluate both methods across multiple-choice, yes/no, open-ended question answering, and mathematical reasoning tasks. Our approach outperforms baselines on most metrics, while LProp achieves the lowest mean inference-token usage in all eight propagation settings. Matched feature ablations further demonstrate that inherited latent content improves error recovery beyond answer probabilities or model capacity alone.

ee1a23c7385f1c82569565a3.title_original: Receiver-Conditioned Clarification for Multi-Agent Food Assistance
ee1a23c7385f1c82569565a3.excerpt: arXiv:2611.23572v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Food insecurity creates a pressing need for guidance that helps households find usable food resources and assess food choices in light of their circumstances. Such guidance must connect eligibility requirements, practical access constraints, and dietary needs rather than return isolated listings or generic nutritional advice. Multi-agent food assistants can coordinate these tasks, with uncertainty indicating when clarification or verification is needed before a recommendation. However, uncertainty can be lost across agent handoffs, allowing tentative interpretations to propagate as facts and obscuring opportunities for correction. Moreover, confidence that a service requirement has been interpreted correctly is not confidence that a recommendation satisfies the user's needs; local confidence cannot simply be reused as downstream reliability. We introduce an inference-time, receiver-conditioned clarification framework that preserves shared premise identities and replays consistent interpretations across dependent agents. Each receiver exposes admissible decisions and remaining evidence obligations, so question relevance reflects both decision changes and missing support. Information questions and user-confirmable fallback adjustments are evaluated together with their anticipated follow-up interactions under shared budgets. This structure connects clarification to jointly supported plans for resource navigation, nutritional reasoning, and supply-side planning.

6fa5dcce00b8e84ea09b2189.title_original: ARISE: Practical Self-Evolving Memory for Accurate and Cost-Efficient Enterprise Agents
6fa5dcce00b8e84ea09b2189.excerpt: arXiv:2611.23588v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Enterprise LLM agents operate in dynamic environments where foundation models evolve rapidly, workflows update frequently, and deployments need to satisfy accuracy and cost requirements. We propose ARISE (Agent Refinement through Iterative Self-Evaluation), a practical memory architecture in which the agent's memory evolves from its own failures without updating model weights, tools, or workflow logic. ARISE uses the model itself or a teacher model to attribute the failures and propose corrections. Then, ARISE keeps the corrections as retrievable micro memory, consolidates them into macro rules, and accepts a rule update only if held-out accuracy rises. Across 14 enterprise-workflow domains from SOP-Bench and $\tau^2$-bench using 5 models, ARISE-Teacher, which uses Claude Opus 4.6 for attribution and consolidation, gains 10.9 pp over the baseline on SOP-Bench and 5.8 pp on $\tau^2$-bench. ARISE-Teacher also outperforms GEPA by 4.5 pp on $\tau^2$-bench and 1.4 pp on SOP-Bench. With the deployment model as its own attributor, ARISE-Self still gains 10.0 pp on SOP-Bench. ARISE-Teacher uses 4.0% fewer model calls and 5.2% fewer output tokens at comparable per-task cost (-1.0%).

c1d7fc81bcb77ab8bf71f86f.title_original: RefinementGuard: Counterexample-Directed Semantic Qualification for Hidden Agent-Tool Execution
c1d7fc81bcb77ab8bf71f86f.excerpt: arXiv:2611.23611v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Tool runtimes can lower an agent-selected operation into a hidden parallel graph, reducing latency and context while risking semantic mistranslation. We introduce RefinementGuard: translation validation for hidden, effectful agent-tool lowerings, coupled to artifact-bound, fail-closed runtime admission. Qualification compares a candidate graph with an independent reference on isolated state using explicit parent-operation obligations. We evaluate two repository-level contracts, bug localization and patch validation, on controlled repositories. Among 100 activated, non-equivalent development/qualification faults adjudicated by one human, parent-semantic validation rejects 49/100 (operator-cluster bootstrap 95% CI [33.7%, 64.8%]). The objective is selective admission, not maximum mutation rejection: exact equality rejects 100/100 faults but also all 60 valid variants, whereas obligation-based validation accepts 60/60; its 51 residual misses identify concrete specification gaps. On a frozen disjoint input split, the held-out B2-B3 result is localization-only because 21 patch mutants fail structurally; B3 rejects 38/56 localization defects. In a controlled asynchronous-delay regime, the localization serial/guarded median-latency ratio is 4.50x, and hidden execution exposes 74.3% less parent-visible context than visible execution. Patch validation shows no demonstrated speedup; zero-delay runs expose overhead. End-to-end qualification thus detects lower-layer misses while preserving localization's parallelism.

c8e80c6b7e924a41136b9f3f.title_original: Searching the Pareto Front: Multi-Objective Retrieval for Heterogeneous Scientific Modalities
c8e80c6b7e924a41136b9f3f.excerpt: arXiv:2611.23639v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In cosmology, surveys span different sky regions and wavelength ranges, resulting in uneven modality coverage across observational datasets. Such heterogeneity can be addressed through either multimodal foundation models (FMs), which learn shared embedding spaces, or independently learned modality embeddings combined via late fusion. We investigate whether the latter provides an adaptive alternative to FM-based scientific retrieval. We evaluate this approach on a galaxy retrieval task spanning diverse modalities--history of star formation, spectra of light emitted, and multi-wavelength observations from two telescopes--comparing an FM baseline with separately trained embeddings fused through multi-objective optimization based on Pareto optimality. We find that the FM baseline achieves strong embedding-space proximity, but our method preserves modality-specific distance structure that allows scientists to inspect which physical signals drive similarity. Our method also achieves improved fidelity in raw-data space: across six measured properties, its nearest neighbor is 8% closer to the query on average than that retrieved by kNN in the FM embedding space (spread 0.128 vs. 0.139). These results suggest that multi-objective retrieval can surface astrophysically coherent candidates that single-objective search alone may overlook.

6a9c07ec64db4c7f3ac14dc9.title_original: Evaluating Governed LLM-Driven ML Experimentation: Lifecycle, Provenance, and Failure Metrics
6a9c07ec64db4c7f3ac14dc9.excerpt: arXiv:2611.23678v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Autonomous agents that run ML experiments are usually judged by the best score they reach. That score says nothing about how it was reached: whether the agent stayed within the files it was allowed to edit, whether failed trials were kept or silently dropped, and whether each keep or discard decision can be traced to its evidence. We propose evaluating such systems on their experimental process as well as their outcome, and we build a governed harness that makes this possible. A control plane, not the LLM that proposes changes, owns each trial's lifecycle, checks its edit scope, decides keep or discard, and appends one record per trial to an append-only ledger. Governance metrics such as the invalid-action rate, the repeated-bad rate and provenance completeness are computed from that ledger. Across six ML tasks, from synthetic logistic regression to language-model training, and 1,445 trials, the same contract applied unchanged. The ledger exposed failures that a task score hides: a no-memory arm in which all 120 trials failed, a benchmark adapter whose bounded proposals ran out, and a reset failure that reproducibility hashes revealed, after which the affected campaigns were rerun. In a matched counterfactual, a loop that logs only successful trials left no record of 43 of 50 trials, while the governed ledger recorded all 50. Memory ablations show that memory's effect on repeated bad proposals depends on the task. We release the ledgers of all 1,445 trials, so that every number reported for them can be recomputed.

1ccd70e157e6071e4a371a7d.title_original: Auditable Clinical Support with Decision Agents
1ccd70e157e6071e4a371a7d.excerpt: arXiv:2611.23700v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Clinicians reviewing a diagnostic work-up will ask what was considered at each step and why the assessment changed. Agents powered by free text can reach physician-level diagnostic accuracy, but their written reasoning does not always reflect the factors that went into the decision. Here, we present Decision2Care, a decision agent that works up the acutely ill patient without producing any text. A decision model assigns a probability to each permitted EHR action, and fixed rules carry out the most probable one. We evaluated Decision2Care on the records of 546 emergency admissions across 12 diseases. Decision2Care reached a diagnostic accuracy of 86.5%, compared with 86.1% for the MIRA-v2 agent, and required a median of 2.2 s per work-up, compared with 92-100 s. Each work-up tracked which options Decision2Care was considering at each step. In 10 of the 12 diseases, the differential diagnosis changed most at the test on which the guideline bases the diagnosis. Where Decision2Care was most confident after a single work-up, all but four of its diagnoses were correct (98.5%). We traced each of these four errors back to a single imaging report. Three of them were corrected when that report was removed. The same kind of decision was used to select the treatments, and Decision2Care's drug orders were judged guideline-adherent more often than MIRA-v2's. In emergency patients, its prediction of death was comparable to that of three intensivists on the same cases. In five of the eight intensive care cohorts, it exceeded the best of the three 24-h severity scores within 2-6 h of records. Our results show that decision agents can carry out clinical work-ups while recording the options, probabilities, and execution rules behind each action for audit.

4857b456b8cfe34bf90b5b9e.title_original: KnowMe Paper Radar: Lightweight Discovery of Promising Papers in the Age of Autoresearch
4857b456b8cfe34bf90b5b9e.excerpt: arXiv:2611.23702v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The growing volume of topically similar papers makes it difficult to identify new work that can offer useful research insights or methodological guidance. We present KnowMe Paper Radar, a lightweight discovery tool that combines multiple sources of evidence into personalized reading priorities. Users specify topics, priorities, exclusions and dates; the system brings together topical relevance, recency, author research histories, collaboration paths and direction-specific institutional context. By exposing each score component and its supporting sources, KnowMe helps readers select promising papers for their current questions and discover relevant work beyond familiar authors. Automatic acquisition, version merging and graph-cache reuse keep this workflow convenient without large language model (LLM) inference during ordinary use. Experiments on 174,640 acquired records show more than threefold faster repeated context preparation, while cached abstracts improve normalized discounted cumulative gain at rank 10 (NDCG@10) from 0.412 to 0.598 on expert-judged retrieval tasks. Complementary analyses examine how the same accumulated records support semantic retrieval, research-history modeling and literature-grounded planning. A browser interface and a structured command-line interface (CLI) make these capabilities available to both researchers and research agents, positioning KnowMe as a practical upstream tool for literature-informed recursive self-improvement (RSI) workflows.

acc6ebc543ddd0d73f6b2519.title_original: Modeling LLM Reasoning Dynamics with Structural Representations
acc6ebc543ddd0d73f6b2519.excerpt: arXiv:2611.23749v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Language-model reasoning alternates between sustained activities and local operations. We study how this temporal structure predicts continuation and the computation needed to analyze it. T/E/S combines text, local events, and spans of activity. Across reasoning and information-seeking tasks, events and spans improve next-outcome prediction in 70 of 76 evaluation groups for a Transformer and 74 of 76 for Qwen with LoRA. Span duration and preceding events are associated with transitions, and retaining event history across span boundaries improves prediction. We formulate budget-allocation counting and action-conditional continuation queries, prove counting hardness under explicit encodings, and derive conditions for affordable decision certification. In finite-process experiments, bounds that cancel shared continuation mass recover the same optimal actions as full dynamic programming while reducing mean inference CPU time by 77.7%. On 71 held-out HotpotQA and MuSiQue questions, a compact structural observer improves prediction of whether a fixed inference procedure finishes within a CPU allowance: Brier loss falls from 0.0836 to 0.0756. An annotation audit identifies substantial errors in that observer, separating this computational result from semantic validation of its features.

d3e44847918848d1add664ab.title_original: Thinking Fast, Anywhere: One System-1 for the Decision Points of Any Agent Workflow
d3e44847918848d1add664ab.excerpt: arXiv:2611.23751v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Autonomous LLM agents incur substantial cost and latency by invoking a large model (System-2) at every step, even when many intermediate actions choose among a small set of known candidates. Existing dual-system agents offload such decisions to a lightweight System-1 model, but rely on workflow-specific hooks authored per environment. We present AnyS1, a framework that turns human-authored procedural skills, whose instructions naturally specify where choices arise and which options apply, into a shared, domain-general source of decision points. Offline, AnyS1 mines grounded enumerable decisions across over 1,000 public skills, gathers execution-grounded trajectory states inside isolated containers to construct Any-DP, and trains a single calibrated 4B pointer System-1 with label smoothing. At run time, compiled workflows resolve routine decisions in one forward pass and fall back to System-2 when confidence falls below a calibrated threshold. Across three unseen benchmarks and distinct System-2 model families, AnyS1 preserves task reliability while cutting episode cost by 75-91% and model-call time by 63-92% relative to an uncompiled System-2 agent, and maintains performance under zero-shot threshold transfer.

a8d3fcb50abe47c4b77c94e7.title_original: Continual Tool-Space Extension Learning for Multimodal Agents
a8d3fcb50abe47c4b77c94e7.excerpt: arXiv:2611.23810v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Multimodal agents largely rely on generic tools such as cropping, search, and code execution, leaving specialist vision models outside their tool space. However, bringing such a model into an already trained agent is not straightforward. The challenge is to learn each new tool efficiently while retaining the ability to use existing ones. This work proposes COTEX, continual tool-space extension learning, that adds new tools at efficient adapter-level cost. COTEX locates two sets of parameter directions; one triggers a tool call and thereby opens a multi-turn reasoning trajectory, while the other determines which tool is chosen. The adapter of a new tool is restricted to the calling directions that leave earlier tool choices unaffected by orthogonal constraint. We further introduce a protocol that converts specialist models' existing task-specific annotations into verified tool-use trajectories. Experiments on two representative agents and three specialist tools show gains on ten vision-language benchmarks, with at most a 0.3-point drop on existing tools.

3bbeb407b25e4b373fc65579.title_original: Metrics-in-the-Loop: Complexity Feedback Reshapes Agent-Written Code
3bbeb407b25e4b373fc65579.excerpt: arXiv:2611.23817v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Coding agents now write whole codebases in long autonomous runs, guided mainly by whether their tests pass. Yet passing tests alone does not reveal accumulating complexity or gaps in test coverage, which then persist as agents extend their own code. We introduce metrics-in-the-loop, an inference-time intervention that gives agents in-flight feedback: cheap, automatically computed code metrics injected into the agent's context during the trajectory. After each code-changing agent turn, we insert short feedback messages naming changed functions whose cyclomatic complexity exceeds a limit (complexity feedback) or changed lines that are skipped by tests (coverage feedback), giving the agent the opportunity to refactor code or strengthen tests before continuing. We run extensive experiments and ablations comparing several interventions across three long-horizon coding benchmarks and four strong models. We find that complexity feedback significantly reduces erosion, a measure of complexity concentration of code, without affecting held-out correctness of the code. Broadly, our experiments investigate a practical form of agent "re-railing", where timely, actionable measurements redirect agents before weaknesses become the foundation they keep building on. As agents scale to codebases with millions of lines, such interventions become critical to sustaining effective development and long-term code maintainability.

14bbcc301e2e34d91038a868.title_original: Evidence-Based Credit Assignment for Search-Augmented Language Models
14bbcc301e2e34d91038a868.excerpt: arXiv:2611.23824v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Reinforcement learning from terminal answer rewards enables search-augmented language models to interleave reasoning and retrieval without step-level annotations, yet outcome supervision assigns identical credit to every search in a trajectory regardless of whether it retrieved useful information. This limitation is especially severe when all sampled rollouts for a question fail, collapsing group-centered outcome advantages to zero even when trajectories gather markedly different evidence. We present Evidence-based Credit Assignment (ECA), which augments terminal outcome rewards with a training-only auxiliary signal measuring how retrieved documents improve the likelihood of a reference answer. Rather than scoring the full dialogue prefix, ECA queries a frozen snapshot of the current policy under an evidence-only prompt containing solely the question and the deduplicated documents observed so far, isolating the utility of retrieved passages from surface variations in generated thoughts or search queries. Within this framework, we compare two return formulations, ECA-Step (which accumulates step-clipped potential increments) and ECA-Horizon (which preserves the telescoping horizon gain in potential), paired with cross-fold group normalization, novelty gating, and search-local token assignment. Across seven Search QA benchmarks, ECA-Horizon improves strict macro exact match over an outcome-only GRPO baseline by 1.03 and 4.80 percentage points on Qwen2.5-3B- and 7B-Instruct, respectively, outperforming both RLOO and GiGPO. Zero-shot evaluation on MultiHop-RAG further demonstrates strong transfer to multi-hop inference queries.

15ce5651a954c9a8bd815be2.title_original: A System 1 Decision Model for Medical Multiple-Choice Questions Built on Frozen Language Models
15ce5651a954c9a8bd815be2.excerpt: arXiv:2611.23832v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A System 1 model answers a multiple-choice question in a single pass. A frozen language model turns the question and each option into vectors, two small, trained heads place them in a shared space, and the closest option wins. The design has been shown on agent decisions, but we are not aware of a study of how far it goes on exam questions that need medical knowledge, where the right option is often no more similar to the question than the wrong ones. We rebuilt the recipe from scratch for MedMCQA and trained only two projection heads and one temperature on top of frozen Qwen3.5-0.8B, Granite-4.2-3B and Qwen3-8B, using a contrastive loss with in-batch and hard negatives and a mask for repeated answers. With plain last-token vectors, both small encoders answer about one question in three correctly (33.1% and 33.0% on 3,842 held-out questions, where chance is 25.0%). Writing each text inside a one-word-summary prompt and lowering the learning rate of the heads raised this to 41.7% and 42.5% for the two small encoders and to 46.0% +-0.2 (three seeds) for Qwen3-8B. Shuffling the questions against the options returns accuracy to chance, so the heads do use the question. Flan-PaLM and Med-PaLM 2 report 57.6% and 72.3% on MedMCQA under a different protocol, so ours is a cheap, fast baseline and not a competitive system. We also say what our evidence cannot show: validation gains were about 1.7 to 2 times the test gains, and we could not separate the effect of reading several encoder layers from the other changes.

0fe8db391afca86d741d0f3d.title_original: RoboBuilder: Agentic Robot Co-Design with Real-world Video Feedback in the Loop
0fe8db391afca86d741d0f3d.excerpt: arXiv:2611.23855v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Can AI agents design robots that work in the real world? We introduce RoboBuilder, a benchmark in which coding agents co-design a robot's hardware and program from standard parts, motors and a custom 3D-printed part, and every design that passes in simulation is built and tested on a physical course. Simulation alone is not enough: under public part data, none of 15 initial passing designs crossed the real course, so an agent learns the simulator from measurements it requests and videos of real runs. Across four frontier coding agents, ten obstacles at three difficulty levels, 16,427 simulations of 12,774 distinct robots and 135 physical robots built in an estimated 240 hours, agents solve nearly all easy obstacles and invent mechanisms our search baselines do not reach, but falter at harder levels, when one robot must cross every obstacle, and in the real world, where 66% of simulated passes hold across all levels. Closing the loop helps: shown a video of its real failure, an agent redesigns the robot, sometimes correcting its simulator, and removes 72% of level-1 and level-2 failures. RoboBuilder measures progress toward agents that engineer real machines. Project Page: https://ghadinehme.com/robobuilder.github.io/

30e9e26fdd22ebaa97cf6c47.title_original: Asking but Missing: Decision Coverage in Natural-Language Data Querying
30e9e26fdd22ebaa97cf6c47.excerpt: arXiv:2611.23864v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models are increasingly used to translate natural language questions about structured data into executable programs. A fundamental challenge is recognizing when a question admits multiple computational interpretations and identifying the decisions needed to resolve them. We investigate whether language models recognize these unresolved decisions before generating code, or silently adopt assumptions that may lead to incorrect results. We refer to the latter behavior as Underspecified Decision Completion (UDC). To distinguish different causes of UDC, we introduce Grounded Code Generation (GCG), a diagnostic protocol that separates the identification of unresolved decisions, their resolution using evidence, and their translation into executable code. By examining each stage separately, we can determine where the decisions responsible for incorrect results were first missed or mishandled. We evaluate this framework on BIRD-Pandas with twelve models. The results show that answering clarification questions consistently improves execution accuracy, yet substantial errors remain. Our findings suggest that the main difficulty lies not in answering clarification questions, but in recognizing which questions need to be asked in the first place.

1c3df0a849ccca2c0bb363b5.title_original: Risk-Controlled Correction for Frozen Multimodal Models under Missing Modalities
1c3df0a849ccca2c0bb363b5.excerpt: arXiv:2611.23886v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A deployed multimodal predictor may face missing modalities after its weights can no longer be changed. This raises a question that training-time repair does not answer: what part of the resulting error is still correctable from the information that remains? We show that this part is characterized by the Bayes gap, the difference between the model's prediction and the Bayes prediction given the observed modalities. For cross-entropy and squared error, excess risk measures this gap in the geometry of the loss; ambiguity in the observed modalities cannot be removed. Thus, a badly degraded prediction is not necessarily a correctable one. Estimating the Bayes prediction normally requires labels. However, when a model observing more modalities is conditionally correct, averaging its outputs conditional on the remaining modalities recovers this target without retrieval labels; with the same fixed blend and neighbors, it is no worse in expected cross-entropy or Brier risk than averaging hard labels. Some such assumption is unavoidable: otherwise the target is not identifiable from unlabeled data alone. GUARD (Gated Utility-Aware Recalibration for Deployment) leaves the deployed predictor unchanged. It estimates a candidate correction by retrieval, learns from deployment-matched labeled data when correction is likely to help, and calibrates a threshold on a held-out split by conformal risk control. Under exchangeability, the marginal probability that GUARD applies a correction whose loss increase exceeds a prescribed tolerance is bounded by a preset level, regardless of the learned score. In controlled experiments, correction gain follows headroom rather than raw error; across nine frozen model-dataset pairs spanning six domains, GUARD retains most of blanket correction's gain within harm budgets that blanket correction often exceeds.

7be869e02db330fee98dd5ed.title_original: EVA-RSI: Recursive Self-Improvement of Video Evaluators for Judging Temporal Quality
7be869e02db330fee98dd5ed.excerpt: arXiv:2611.23890v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Video evaluators play an important role in video generation, yet they miss motion defects, limiting the quality of generated videos. Recursive self-improvement (RSI) has made strong progress in mathematics and coding, where explicit verifiers provide reliable feedback on a single goal. Video evaluation poses two difficulties for RSI: it has no verifier, and it must judge many dimensions at once, such as physics, smoothness and dynamics, where a gain on one can cost another. We introduce EVA-RSI, a multi-agent framework for exploring RSI under these two constraints. We build a fixed proxy exam with construction-defined targets by applying controlled changes to videos, such as temporal reversal and frame dropping. These edits supply supervision without human annotation. A small set of human-labeled real videos anchors the exam to human judgment. Each dimension has an LLM agent that proposes improvements. A leader agent coordinates the proposals, and a Nash bargaining rule selects updates that balance progress across dimensions. Humans design the exam, review candidate changes and revise the curriculum between stages. Starting from Qwen3-VL-8B, EVA-RSI improves motion evaluation, with the largest gain on smoothness, and the gains carry over to defect types never seen during the run. On the dynamics subsets of public benchmarks, our evaluator achieves the highest observed scores among 21 tested models. As an RL reward, it increases generated motion and earns human preference. A data-selection pipeline incorporating it also increases motion.

b2471871116893a9a252c9cc.title_original: Evaluating invariance training with certified answer-changing controls in neural graph algorithms
b2471871116893a9a252c9cc.excerpt: arXiv:2611.23907v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Invariance training aims to make neural algorithmic reasoners robust to answer-preserving input changes and is judged by accuracy and by how rarely such edits change predictions. We ask whether this evaluation detects lost sensitivity to answer-changing edits on minimum spanning trees of synthetic graphs, where both directions can be certified. Attaching a subgraph through one bridge provably preserves every original label. Attaching it through two edges, oracle-selected to change a label, and lowering one weight inside the graph serve as answer-changing controls; a response is a changed prediction on an edge whose label changes. A reproduced graph transformer (GDT) within its published accuracy range changes a provably fixed label on 53.3-65.9% of the 64-vertex graphs it solves exactly after a 64-vertex bridge attachment; removing the connecting edge changes little. With 16-vertex graphs and attachments, three invariance objectives lower GDT violations from 2.91% to 0.52-2.02% of pairs at essentially unchanged accuracy. Training also lowers the response to two-edge attachments from 97.6% to 66.0-79.0%, while the response to in-base weight edits stays near 99.5%. At 64 vertices accuracy also falls, but on 16-vertex bases only the attachment control reveals the loss. A message-passing network loses some attachment response at small penalty weights but gains little invariance. Running the conventionally trained GDT on each biconnected block separately removes all observed violations and keeps accuracy and both responses, so the task does not force the trade-off. Sensitivity checks for trained invariance should include certified answer-changing edits that attach material as the training edits do.

cb818117b1c9807270321212.title_original: Training-Free Domain Generation for One-Shot Federated Learning with Server-Side Pre-trained Diffusion Models
cb818117b1c9807270321212.excerpt: arXiv:2611.23908v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: One-shot federated learning (OSFL) has attracted increasing attention for its ability to substantially reduce communication overhead by limiting client-server interaction to a single communication round. Nevertheless, this limited interaction makes learning from heterogeneous client distributions challenging. Diffusion-based OSFL approaches seek to address this challenge by synthesizing data that approximate client distributions. However, existing diffusion-based approaches often impose substantial computational costs on clients and lack effective visual guidance to generate data aligned with client distributions. To address these limitations, we propose FedDoG, a training-free Domain Generation framework that leverages server-side pre-trained diffusion models to synthesize data aligned with client domains. FedDoG extracts compact domain representations using a frozen image encoder, substantially reducing client-side computational and communication costs. These representations are incorporated into the diffusion model through a pre-trained image-conditioning adapter, thereby providing explicit visual guidance for domain generation. To further improve the quality of synthetic data, FedDoG adapts the strength of visual conditioning according to domain concentration and filters generated samples based on class consistency and predictive entropy. Experiments on three benchmarks demonstrate that FedDoG generates higher-quality synthetic images and outperforms existing OSFL baselines in classification accuracy. Meanwhile, FedDoG reduces client upload and computation time by 99.9% and 91.5%, respectively. The code is available at https://github.com/YXTong17/FedDoG.

ba50fe61261aaf7092c9ae8e.title_original: MLE Agents: Autonomous ML Engineering in Large-scale Recommendation Systems
ba50fe61261aaf7092c9ae8e.excerpt: arXiv:2611.23910v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The typical workflow for improving large-scale ranking and recommendation models is slow and tedious: an engineer forms a hypothesis, implements it as a code change, trains a model, and evaluates it both offline and online, often relying on their own intuition and experience along the way. Autonomous LLM agents promise to speed this up by running the loop on their own, but it is still unclear whether they can do this in industry-scale systems rather than on benchmarks or small proxy tasks. We build human-on-the-loop machine learning engineer (MLE) agents that propose, implement, train, and evaluate model changes on large-scale search rankers. Engineers retain control over objective design, search direction, and final-model review. We identify three obstacles that make this industry setting challenging: feedback takes hours per experiment, offline metrics do not always predict online impact, and improvements saturate after the early wins. We address these with parallel training runs, an objective calibrated to match online impact, and careful context engineering. In one campaign, the system ran 1,097 completed candidate experiments and accepted 325, a 29.6\% acceptance rate compared with 15.6\% in the earlier campaign under a different objective and search constraint. Its best model increases search volume by 0.23\% in an A/B test of large scale. Several improvements were architectural changes the team had never tried, drawn from the broader industry and literature, suggesting that MLE agents can explore regions of the design space that human intuition overlooks. We find that the design of the harness around the model matters: intuition suggests that a stronger underlying model is enough, but in our experience, the design of the loop around it is just as critical. More broadly, our work shows that autonomous agents can do real machine-learning engineering in industry-scale systems.

bb8ee524c99d18aa6c3df107.title_original: Vanguard: Knowing When to Trust the Draft in Speculative Vision-Language Agents
bb8ee524c99d18aa6c3df107.excerpt: arXiv:2611.23917v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Vision-language agents that browse websites, operate phones and act in homes reason before every action, so every step waits for a large model, a latency and cost that stand in the way of deployment. Step-level speculation lets a small model draft each step and calls the large model only on rejected drafts, but its outcome rests on the judge, and a judge that reads only a step's text cannot tell whether the step fits the screen it acts on. We find that a few samples of a small model can contain a correct step about as often as the large model gets the step right, and not always on the same steps: checked against the screen, small drafts can be not only cheaper but better. We present Vanguard, a training-free judge that leaves the draft and target models unchanged: a general decision model, with the screenshot in view, gives each candidate step a probability of being right in one forward pass; the best candidate is kept if it clears a threshold, and otherwise the large model writes the step. On web, mobile and embodied agents, a 2B draft judged by Vanguard is at least as accurate as its 8B target and significantly more accurate on Mind2Web and EB-ALFRED, while the target writes only a minority of the steps; it completes far more closed-loop episodes, and with a 27B target from another family it is both faster and more accurate. Vanguard is the most accurate judge we compare on the agent tasks; it relies on the screenshot on web and mobile tasks, its calibrated threshold transfers to unseen websites, and across model families its gain over the target grows with the draft's pass@4 relative to the target's accuracy. Vanguard composes with token-level speculative decoding and matches trained process reward models on mathematics, turning speculation from a way to save the large model's work into one that can improve on it.

c76a6ba89a723b7a5cdca3f7.title_original: Cardiac MRI-informed electrocardiography enables biologically grounded cardiomyopathy detection
c76a6ba89a723b7a5cdca3f7.excerpt: arXiv:2611.23925v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Precise myocardial phenotyping at population scale is limited by the cost and accessibility of cardiac magnetic resonance (CMR), whereas electrocardiography (ECG) is widely available but reflects electrical rather than structural and functional information. Here we develop MyoECG, a cross-modal representation learning framework that distils myocardial structural and functional knowledge from CMR into standard 12-lead ECGs, enabling imaging-informed cardiomyopathy detection and subtype classification from ECGs alone. MyoECG was pretrained on 45,241 paired ECG-CMR examinations from UK Biobank and a tertiary cardiovascular centre, then developed and validated across more than 1.8 million ECGs from seven independent datasets. Across internal and external datasets spanning prevalences of 0.2-54.7%, MyoECG outperformed five pretrained ECG foundation models, with AUROCs of 0.800-0.974 for cardiomyopathy detection. In a multi-reader study of six cardiologists, MyoECG assistance improved mean sensitivity by 0.109 (95% CI, 0.041-0.175; P = 0.009) and specificity by 0.056 (95% CI, 0.004-0.108; P = 0.040). In 41,128 UK Biobank participants, the MyoECG score showed genetic correlations with cardiomyopathy (rg = 0.409) and dilated cardiomyopathy (rg = 0.371), genome-wide associations at four loci, including regions mapped to NFIA and KCNQ1, and associations with 69 circulating proteins related to myocardial stress, cell adhesion, vascular biology and metabolism. The cardiomyopathy correlation attenuated to non-significance after adjustment for 27 measured CMR traits (rg = 0.131; P = 0.143), indicating that the score captures CMR-derived information rather than dataset-specific shortcuts. MyoECG offers a scalable route to CMR-informed cardiomyopathy assessment and a strategy for transferring knowledge from resource-intensive imaging to widely deployable physiological signals.

36557b1055bd26310baa0eb7.title_original: Can you make models believe false facts in the prompt?
36557b1055bd26310baa0eb7.excerpt: arXiv:2611.23938v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Making LLMs believe false facts is useful for alignment evaluations and for building model organisms. Previous work explored doing so with Synthetic Document Finetuning (SDF). But SDF requires fine-tuning one new model for each set of injected false beliefs. To enable larger scale SDF-powered alignment evaluations, we attempt to produce a single model that believes any fact placed in a tag in the prompt. To do so, we explore doing prompt-conditioned SDF: fine-tuning a model on synthetic documents covering thousands of facts, with each document conditioned on a fact presented in the prompt. We evaluate how deeply the model believes the facts provided in the prompt using evaluations from prior work and a new Jacobian lens evaluation. We find that the belief depth on unseen facts scales roughly log-linearly with the number of training facts, making this a cheap, promising avenue for making models believe false facts, though preliminary experiments on applying it to alignment audits on the small model we studied showed negative results due to these small models often already acting as if they believed facts provided in regular honeypot system prompts. Using RL to reduce the rate at which models verbalize following a false fact in the prompt, on top of prompt-conditioned SDF, generalizes to held-out evals and almost matches SDF on some evaluations. But training against one of our metrics for belief depth makes it harder to trust those evaluations.

f50562079134bf85f39fcf88.title_original: GLIDE: Scalable and Event-Aware Inductive Forecasting over Evolving Logistics Graphs
f50562079134bf85f39fcf88.excerpt: arXiv:2611.23942v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Accurate forecasting of order volume at scale-effect hotspots (SEHs), spatially coherent groups of logistics flows that serve as distributed optimization units for real-time many-to-one dispatch, is a prerequisite for efficient order pooling in on-demand food delivery (OFD) platforms such as Meituan. However, real-world logistics networks present unique challenges that render standard spatiotemporal prediction model ineffective. (i) Dynamic Topology: Unlike static road networks, logistics graphs are ephemeral, with hotspot emerging and vanishing continuously; (ii) Scale--Volume Heterogeneity: Graph sizes vary from $10^2$ to $10^4$, while zero-inflated, long-tailed volumes create computational bottlenecks and bias predictions toward inactivity; and (iii) Event-Driven Disruption: Exogenous events (holidays, weather, academic calendars) induce systematic demand shifts that purely data-driven backbones cannot anticipate. In this paper, we present GLIDE, a production-ready framework that models evolving logistics graphs in a scalable latent space while adapting to heterogeneous demand regimes and event-driven shifts. GLIDE introduces a Graph-Guided Latent Aggregation mechanism, which dynamically projects varying physical subgraphs into a fixed-size, semantically stable latent space via a differentiable sparse assignment...

f648fbbad8d16fd403c9b878.title_original: SCAFFOLD: Toward Warrant-Preserving Evidence Transport for Reusable LLM-Agent Skills
f648fbbad8d16fd403c9b878.excerpt: arXiv:2611.23990v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: An agent skill that succeeded yesterday may be executable today without being justified for reuse today. Tests may cover only observable contract clauses, outcome oracles may be absent, evaluations may inherit the same erroneous specification, and permissions or dependencies may change between validation and invocation. We argue that the appropriate unit of prospective trust is a Warranted Reuse Claim (WRC): a defeasible, claim-specific authorization tied to a versioned skill, target context, evidence, assumptions, and identified defeaters. The paper sharpens this position through Warrant-Preserving Evidence Transport (WPET), a proposed discipline for deciding which historical evidence remains admissible after context change. It distinguishes evidence admissibility from truth of the supported safety or effectiveness claim; states a conditional preservation result and its limits; specifies three-valued applicability and asymmetric context-transfer judgments; and illustrates how provenance dependence and policy-invalidating changes alter authorization. We explicitly relate the proposal to assurance cases, contracts, and skill-library maintenance rather than claiming novelty for their ingredients.
